speaker: Devi
title: Opening Scripture and Source
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
श्रुतं देि मया सिं रुद्रयामलसम्भवम् ।
विकभेदमशेषेण सारात्सारविभागश् ॥ १ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava-tantram |
vijñānabhairava-tantram |
śrutaṃ devi mayā samyak rudrayāmala-sambhavam |
vikalpabhedam aśeṣeṇa sārāt sāravibhāgaśaḥ || 1 ||
translation: The Vijñānabhairava Tantra, the Vijñānabhairava Tantra. O Devi, I have heard fully the scripture born of the Rudrayāmala, divided without remainder into distinctions, with its essence extracted from essence.
intent_summary: Devi introduces the scripture and frames it as a distilled teaching meant to reveal its essential meaning.
beginner_explanation: This verse is not yet a practice; it is an opening statement that presents the text as a concentrated teaching. Devi says she has heard the Tantra and wants the essential point, not just many different explanations. It is like asking for the heart of a long book in plain words.
scholar_explanation: This is a framing verse, not a dhāraṇā. Devi invokes the Rudrayāmala-derived Vijñānabhairava as a text of sārāt-sāra-vibhāga, an extraction of the essence from divisive conceptuality (vikalpa-bheda). The verse establishes the pedagogical aim of the dialogue: to move from textual plurality to nondual realization.

speaker: Devi
title: Inquiry into Bhairava's True Nature
sanskrit:
अद्यावप न निवृत्तो मे संशयः परमेश्वर ।
किं रूपं तत्त्वतो देि शब्दराशिकलामयम् ॥ २ ॥
transliteration:
adyāpi na nivṛtto me saṃśayaḥ parameśvara |
kiṃ rūpaṃ tattvato deva śabdarāśikalāmayam || 2 ||
translation: Even now, my doubt has not been dispelled, O Supreme Lord. What is your true form, O Deva, in reality—made of the mass of sound, syllables, and articulations?
intent_summary: Devi asks Bhairava to disclose his real nature beyond conceptual descriptions.
beginner_explanation: Devi is saying, “I still don’t understand what you really are.” She asks whether Bhairava is some kind of reality made of sound, syllables, or energy. In simple terms, she wants to know what the deepest truth is behind appearances.
scholar_explanation: Devi’s question targets Bhairava’s tattva, asking whether his rūpa is śabda-rāśi-kalā-maya—composed of sonic, phonemic, or subtle articulatory powers. The inquiry gestures toward the Tantric doctrine that the ultimate is both beyond and immanent in vibratory manifestation. This sets up Bhairava’s response that the real nature is nondual and not reducible to categories.

speaker: Devi
title: Is Bhairava Divided or Unified?
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वकं वा निात्मभेदेन भैरवे भैरवाकृतौ ।
विवशरोभेदवभन्नं वा वकं वा शविियात्मकम् ॥ ३ ॥
transliteration:
kiṃ vā nirātma-bhedena bhairave bhairavākṛtau |
viveśa-roha-bhedena vibhinnaṃ vā kiṃ vā śivātmakam || 3 ||
translation: Or is Bhairava, in Bhairava’s own form, divided by a distinction of selflessness? Or is he split by entering and rising distinctions? Or is he essentially Śiva?
intent_summary: Devi probes whether Bhairava is a divided entity or an undivided Śiva-nature.
beginner_explanation: Here Devi is trying to understand whether Bhairava is made of separate parts or whether he is really one indivisible reality. She asks in several ways because the mystery is hard to phrase. The point is to know whether the divine is fragmented or whole.
scholar_explanation: The verse explores possible modes of bheda, questioning whether Bhairava’s bhairavākṛti can be interpreted through nirātma-bheda or through transitions of ‘entering’ and ‘rising’ (perhaps alluding to subtle experiential states). The final alternative, śivātmakam, points to identification with Śiva as pure consciousness. This is characteristic of the text’s method: negating dualistic partitions in favor of nondual identity.

speaker: Devi
title: Is He Sound, Sun, Moon, or Power?
sanskrit:
नादविन्दुमयं िावप वकं चन्द्राधधवनरोवधका् ।
चक्रारूढमनच्कं वा वकं वा शविस्वरूपकम् ॥ ४ ॥
transliteration:
nāda-bindumayaṃ vāpi kiṃ candrādhi-nirodhikāḥ |
cakrārūḍham anacchaṃ vā kiṃ vā śakti-svarūpakam || 4 ||
translation: Or is he made of sound and bindu? Or of the moon and the moon’s restraint? Or mounted on a wheel, pure and without obstruction? Or is he of the nature of Śakti herself?
intent_summary: Devi continues to test whether Bhairava can be described through Tantric symbols like sound, bindu, lunar processes, and power.
beginner_explanation: Devi is listing sacred images and asking if Bhairava is any of them. She mentions sound, subtle drops of energy, the moon, a wheel, and divine power. She is really asking: “Which symbol points to your actual nature?”
scholar_explanation: This verse expands the inquiry into Tantric iconography and subtle physiology: nāda-bindu, candra and candra-nirodhikā, cakra, and śakti-svarūpa. The series of options shows that Bhairava exceeds symbolic forms while also being expressible through them. In Kashmiri Śaivism, such images often function as supports for recognition (pratyabhijñā), not final definitions.

speaker: Devi
title: Beyond Para and Apara
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
परापरायाः सकलम् अपरायाश्च वा पुनः ।
पराया यदि तद्वत्स्यात् परत्वं तद् विरुध्यते ॥ ५ ॥
transliteration:
parāparāyāḥ sakalam aparāyāś ca vā punaḥ |
parā yadi tadvat syāt paratvaṃ tad virudhyate || 5 ||
translation: Is he all of the higher and the lower, or only the lower? If he were only the higher in that way, then his being supreme would be contradicted.
intent_summary: Devi questions whether Bhairava belongs to the highest state, the lower state, or both, and notes the contradiction in making him only one pole.
beginner_explanation: Devi is asking whether the divine includes both the highest and lowest levels of reality. If you say he is only the highest, that seems too limited. She is testing whether the truth is bigger than neat categories.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses the para/apara distinction, central to Tantric cosmology, to problematize any exclusive attribution. If Bhairava were only parā, his paratva would paradoxically be limited by exclusion. The verse prepares the nondual resolution that the supreme includes and transcends all graded manifestations.

speaker: Devi
title: Beyond Letters and Bodies
sanskrit:
न हि वर्णविभेदेन देहभेदेन वा भवेत् ।
परत्वम् निष्कलत्वेन सकलत्वे न तद्भवेत् ॥ ६ ॥
transliteration:
na hi varṇa-vibhedena deha-bhedena vā bhavet |
paratvaṃ niṣkalatvena sakalatve na tad bhavet || 6 ||
translation: For supremacy cannot exist through distinctions of letters or through distinctions of bodies. If it is without parts, then it cannot be in a state of parts.
intent_summary: Devi argues that the ultimate cannot be divided by language or embodied form if it is truly supreme.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the highest reality cannot be chopped up by letters, labels, or physical forms. If something is truly beyond parts, you should not think of it as being made of separate pieces. It is a way of clearing away limited ideas.
scholar_explanation: Devi rejects varṇa-bheda and deha-bheda as valid grounds for paratva. The logic is precise: if the supreme is niṣkala, it cannot simultaneously be treated as sakala in a literal partitioned sense. This sets up Bhairava’s answer that the totality of experience is his mode of display, while remaining beyond conceptual division.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Grants the Inquiry
sanskrit:
प्रसादं कुरु मे नाथ विशेषं विवि संशयम् ।
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
साधु साधु त्वया पृष्टं तन्त्रसारवमदं प्रिये ॥ ७ ॥
transliteration:
prasādaṃ kuru me nātha viśeṣeṇa vimiśaṃ śamam |
vijñānabhairava-tantram |
sādhu sādhu tvayā pṛṣṭaṃ tantra-sāram idaṃ priye || 7 ||
translation: Lord, bestow your grace upon me; especially still this confusion and doubt. Well done, well done—dear one, you have asked about the essence of the Tantra.
intent_summary: Bhairava blesses Devi’s question and confirms that she has asked the central issue.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava responds kindly and says her question is good. He asks for grace to clear up confusion and praises her for asking about the heart of the teaching. This is like a teacher saying, “Yes, you’ve asked exactly the right thing.”
scholar_explanation: Bhairava begins with prasāda, indicating that understanding is not merely intellectual but a grace-mediated recognition. By calling the query tantra-sāra, he confirms that Devi has moved beyond superficial doctrine to the core of practice. The affectionate address ‘priye’ also reflects the intimate dialogical style typical of nondual Tantra.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Hidden Teaching is Revealed
sanskrit:
गूहनीयतमं भद्रे तथावप कथयावम ते ।
यविंवचत्सकलम् रूपम् भैरवस्य प्रकीर्तितम् ॥ ८ ॥
transliteration:
gūhanīyatamaṃ bhadre tathāpi kathayāmi te |
yad vijñānaṃ sakalaṃ rūpaṃ bhairavasya prakīrtitam || 8 ||
translation: O gentle one, although it is most secret, I shall still tell you: the knowledge by which the entire manifested form of Bhairava is proclaimed.
intent_summary: Bhairava says he will reveal the secret knowledge through which all of Bhairava’s manifested form is understood.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says this teaching is very private, but he will share it. He explains that there is a kind of knowing that lets you recognize Bhairava in everything that appears. It is not just theory; it is a way of seeing.
scholar_explanation: The verse identifies vijñāna as the key to recognizing sakala-rūpa as Bhairava’s manifestation. ‘Secret’ here does not mean inaccessible but directly experiential and safeguarded from reduction to mere discourse. This introduces the practical orientation of the text: direct methods that disclose the nondual presence of Bhairava in all forms.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Worldly Appearance is Insubstantial
sanskrit:
तदसारतया देवि विज्ञेयं शक्रजालित् ।
मायास्वप्नोपमं चैव गन्धर्वनगरभ्रमम् ॥ ९ ॥
transliteration:
tad asāratayā devi vijñeyaṃ śakrajālit |
māyā-svapnopamaṃ caiva gandharva-nagara-bhramam || 9 ||
translation: O Devi, that should be known as essenceless, like a magical illusion, like a dream, and like the भ्रम of a city of gandharvas.
intent_summary: Bhairava teaches that ordinary appearances are to be seen as insubstantial and dreamlike.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says the world of ordinary appearances is not as solid as it seems. It is like a magic trick, a dream, or a mirage city that appears but has no lasting substance. Seeing this loosens the grip of everyday confusion.
scholar_explanation: This verse uses classic similes—śakrajāla, māyā-svapna, gandharva-nagara—to mark phenomenal reality as lacking inherent essence (asāra). The point is not nihilism but de-reification: appearances are seen as dependent and transient, which clears the way for recognition of the nondual ground. Such imagery is common in Śaiva and Buddhist contemplative literatures alike.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Conceptual Thought as a Reflection Aid
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ध्यानाथं भ्रान्तिबुद्धीनाम् वक्रयाडम्बरवर्तधनाम् ।
केवलं वर्णितं पुंसां विकल्पवनहतात्मनाम् ॥ १० ॥
transliteration:
dhyānārthaṃ bhrānti-buddhīnām vakrāyāmbara-vartmanām |
kevalaṃ varṇitaṃ puṃsāṃ vikalpa-vanahātmanām || 10 ||
translation: For the purpose of meditation, it has been described merely for those whose minds are deluded, whose paths are crooked and troublesome, and whose nature is entangled in conceptual thought.
intent_summary: Bhairava says the preliminary descriptions are only for minds still bound by confusion and concepts.
beginner_explanation: He explains that these descriptions are like training wheels. They are useful for people who are still caught in complicated thoughts and need a way in. Once the mind is steadier, the teaching points beyond words.
scholar_explanation: The verse downgrades discursive description to an upāya for bhrānti-buddhi and vikalpa-vanaha—minds entangled in conceptual thickets. This preserves the distinction between provisional instruction and direct realization, a hallmark of nondual Tantra. The term dhyānārtham shows that even conceptual discourse may function as a support for meditation rather than an end in itself.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Not the Aggregate of Words
sanskrit:
तत्त्वतो न निजात्मासौ शब्दराशिर्न भैरवः ।
न चासौ विविधो देवो न च शक्तिसमात्मकः ॥ ११ ॥
transliteration:
tattvato na nijātmāsau śabdarāśir na bhairavaḥ |
na cāsau vividho devo na ca śaktisamātmakaḥ || 11 ||
translation: In truth, that is not the self, nor is Bhairava merely a mass of words; nor is he a manifold deity, nor one composed of powers as separate elements.
intent_summary: Negate all limited conceptions of Bhairava so the practitioner does not mistake language, multiplicity, or attributes for the absolute.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the ultimate reality is not something you can reduce to words or a list of qualities. It is bigger than any description of a god with separate parts or powers. The point is to stop grasping at labels and look for what cannot be captured by them.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava is defined apophatically: he is not nijātmā as an objectified self, not a śabdarāśi, and not a deva divisible into multiplicity. The denial of śakti as a composite also blocks any dualistic reading in which consciousness and power are separable. This prepares the student for non-conceptual recognition rather than theological objectification.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Nādabindu and Chakras
sanskrit:
नादबिन्दुमयो वापि न चन्द्रार्धनिरोधिका् ।
न चक्रक्रमसम्भिन्नो न च शक्तिस्वरूपकः ॥ १२ ॥
transliteration:
nādabindumayo vāpi na candrārdhanirodhikā |
na cakrakramasambhinno na ca śaktisvarūpakaḥ || 12 ||
translation: Nor is he made of nada and bindu; nor is he the crescent moon's restraint; nor is he divided by the sequence of chakras; nor is he merely the form of power.
intent_summary: Reject subtle yogic maps and symbols as final definitions of Bhairava, even when they are spiritually refined.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that even subtle meditation experiences and energy diagrams are not the whole truth. Sounds, lights, and chakra patterns can be helpful, but they are still only pointers. Don’t confuse the map with the destination.
scholar_explanation: The text negates nāda-bindu, candra-ardha-nirodhikā, cakra-kramas, and śakti-svarūpaka to prevent reification of yogic phenomenology. These are valid supports in tantric sādhana, but not the essence of Bhairava, who transcends all structured manifestations. The teaching is consistent with VBT's insistence on immediate recognition beyond mediate yogic constructs.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Text of the Deluded
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अप्रिुद्धमतीनाम् वह एता िालविभीवषका् ।
मातृमोदकित्सिं प्रिृत्त्यथधमुदाहृतम् ॥ १३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
aprīddhamatīnāṃ vāhetaḥ śālavibhīṣaṇāḥ |
mātṛmodakitsilaṃ pravṛttyartham udāhṛtam || 13 ||
translation: This Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra is proclaimed for the sake of activity, as a terrifying display for minds that are not yet awakened, like a plaything to entice children.
intent_summary: Explain that the teaching uses provisional forms and dramatic language to engage immature minds and guide them toward practice.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the text is designed to meet people where they are. It uses striking images and methods to draw in a distracted mind, like giving a child something appealing so it will come closer. The deeper goal is to lead the mind beyond such supports.
scholar_explanation: The verse characterizes the tantra as an upāya for aprabuddha-mati, employing śālavibhīṣaṇā-like pedagogical devices and mātṛ-modaka imagery. Its aim is pravṛtti in the sense of initiating engagement, not final doctrinal completion. Thus the scripture self-consciously frames itself as a skillful means toward realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Time and Place
sanskrit:
वदक्कालकलनोन्मुिा देशोद्देशाविशेवषणी ।
व्यपदेष्टुमशक्यासािकथ्या परमाथधत् ॥ १४ ॥
transliteration:
vāk-kāla-kalanonmuktā deśoddeśaviśeṣiṇī |
vyapadeṣṭum aśakyā sā kathyā paramārthataḥ || 14 ||
translation: She is free from the constructions of speech and time, and distinct from all places and directions; in truth, she cannot be spoken of or designated.
intent_summary: Point to ultimate reality as beyond speech, time, and spatial localization, making clear that it cannot be fully named.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the deepest reality is not located somewhere, and it does not fit into ordinary language or clocks. You cannot point to it like a place on a map. The practice is to sense what remains when those mental labels fall away.
scholar_explanation: Paramārtha is described as vāk-kāla-kalana-unmukta and deśa-uddeśa-viśeṣinī, indicating transcendence of discursive and spatiotemporal determination. Because it is aśakyā vyapadeṣṭum, language can only gesture toward it via negation. This aligns with the non-conceptual disclosure central to Trika and VBT.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairavī as Inner Bliss
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अन्त् स्वानुभिानन्दा विकल्पोन्मुिगोचरा ।
यावस्था भवरताकारा भैरवी भैरवात्मन् ॥ १५ ॥
transliteration:
antaḥsvānubhavānandā vikalponmuktagocarā |
yāvasthā bhairatākārā bhairavī bhairavātmanā || 15 ||
translation: That state, whose field is free of thought-constructs and whose essence is inner experience and bliss, whose form is Bhairava, is Bhairavī, the self of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Describe the living, blissful, nonconceptual state in which Bhairavī and Bhairava are recognized as one reality.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a deep inner joy that comes when thinking stops dominating experience. It is not excitement from outside things, but a quiet fullness felt from within. In that state, the feminine and masculine divine are not separate—they are one awareness.
scholar_explanation: Bhairavī here is defined as antaḥsvānubhava-ānanda and vikalpa-unmukta-gocara, indicating a direct, non-conceptual mode of realization. Her bhairavatā-ākāra shows that śakti is not other than Bhairava but the radiant modality of his own awareness. The verse collapses any dualism between consciousness and energy into a single experiential fullness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Unsullied All-Pervading Reality
sanskrit:
तद्वपुस्तत्त्वतो ज्ञेयं विमलं विश्वपूरणम् ।
एवं विधे परे तत्त्वे क् पूज्य् कश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १६ ॥
transliteration:
tad vapuḥ tattvato jñeyaṃ vimalaṃ viśvapūraṇam |
evaṃ vidhe pare tattve kaḥ pūjyaḥ kaś ca tṛpyati || 16 ||
translation: That body should be known in truth as stainless and pervading the universe. In such a supreme reality, who is to be worshiped, and who is there to be satisfied?
intent_summary: Direct the practitioner to recognize all-pervading pure reality, where worshiper, worshiped, and fulfillment lose their separate meanings.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the ultimate presence is pure and fills everything. If everything is already that reality, there is no separate object to worship and no separate person to be satisfied. It invites you to rest in wholeness instead of splitting experience into parts.
scholar_explanation: The tattva is vimala and viśva-pūraṇa, indicating a pure, all-encompassing consciousness-body. In such paratattva, conventional ritual categories collapse: pūjya and tṛpti presuppose duality that is absent here. The verse is a direct statement of nondual completion that undercuts ritual externality while preserving its inner significance.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Highest as Devi
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एवं विधा भैरवस्य यावस्था पवरगीयते ।
सा परा पररूपेण परा देवी प्रकीवतधता ॥ १७ ॥
transliteration:
evaṃ vidho bhairavasya yāvasthā parigīyate |
sā parā pararūpeṇa parā devī prakīrtitā || 17 ||
translation: The state of Bhairava that is thus celebrated is that supreme Devi, spoken of as the highest in the form of the supreme.
intent_summary: Identify Bhairava's supreme state with Devi herself, affirming the unity of the divine polarities.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the highest state called Bhairava is also called Devi. In other words, the two divine names point to one reality seen from different angles. The goal is to recognize that the sacred masculine and feminine are not separate.
scholar_explanation: The parigīta avasthā of Bhairava is explicitly identified with parā Devī in parārūpa, a classic Trika move that seals the unity of Śiva and Śakti. The verse shows that names and gendered divine forms are functional designations for one nondual ground. It deepens the prior apophatic descriptions by reasserting identity at the level of realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Śiva and Śakti as One
sanskrit:
शविशविमतोयधद्वद् अभेद् सिधदा वस्थत् ।
अतस्तद्धमधवमधत्वात् पराशवि् परात्मन् ॥ १८ ॥
transliteration:
śivaśaktimato yadyad abheda-siddha-vastutāt |
atastad dharma-dharmitvāt parā śaktiḥ parātmanā || 18 ||
translation: Whatever is possessed of Śiva and Śakti is established as non-different in reality; therefore, because of the relation of attribute and possessor, the supreme Śakti is the supreme Self.
intent_summary: Teach that Śiva and Śakti are inseparable and that the supreme power is identical with the supreme self.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that what looks like two things—consciousness and energy—is actually one reality. Just as a fire and its heat are not really separate, Śiva and Śakti belong together. Realizing this helps you stop dividing your own awareness into pieces.
scholar_explanation: The text argues from abheda-siddha-vastutā: whatever is śiva-śakti-mat is already non-different in fact. The dharma-dharmi relation is then used not to split them but to show that parā śakti is parātman, a hallmark of Trika metaphysics. This formulation supports the VBT's practice methods by grounding them in ontological nonduality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Recognition in Pure Being
sanskrit:
न िह्नेदाधवहका शविव्यधवतवरिा विभाव्यते ।
केिलम् ज्ञानसत्तायां प्रारम्भोऽयं प्रिेशने ॥ १९ ॥
transliteration:
na vahnedhārdhika śakti vyatiriktā vibhāvyate |
kevalam jñāna-sattāyāṃ prārambho 'yaṃ praveśane || 19 ||
translation: The power is not conceived as separate from the fire; this is merely the beginning, a प्रवेश into the state of pure knowledge and being.
intent_summary: Indicate that śakti is inseparable from consciousness and that this teaching is only an entry point into direct knowing.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses the example of fire and heat: they are different aspects of one thing, not two separate things. In the same way, divine power is not apart from consciousness. The verse also says this is only the beginning of the path into direct awareness.
scholar_explanation: The fire-heat analogy denies any real vyatireka between śakti and the conscious principle. Jñāna-sattā here points to the luminous being-character of awareness that becomes accessible through entry (praveśana) rather than discursive inference. The verse functions as a bridge from doctrine to practice.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering Śakti to Become Śiva
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
शक्त्यिस्थाप्रविष्टस्य वनविधभागेन भावना ।
तदासौ वशिरूपी स्यात् शैिी मुखवमहोच्यते ॥ २० ॥
transliteration:
śaktyavasthāpraviṣṭasya nirvibhāgena bhāvanā |
tadāsau śivarūpī syāt śaivī mukham ihocyate || 20 ||
translation: For one who has entered the state of Śakti, contemplation without division arises; then that one becomes of Śiva's nature. This is here called the Śaiva entry-point.
intent_summary: Show that by entering undivided contemplative absorption in śakti, the practitioner realizes Śiva-nature.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that if you settle into the living energy of experience without splitting it up, your mind can become quiet and transparent. In that undivided state, you recognize yourself as Śiva, not as a separate little self. It is like sinking into the ocean and discovering you were never outside it.
scholar_explanation: Śakty-avasthā-praviṣṭa implies immersion in the mode of śakti, and nirvibhāgena bhāvanā indicates undivided contemplative apprehension. The result, śivarūpī syāt, names a transformative recognition rather than a produced state. This is the śaivī mukha, one of the VBT's signature entryways into realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Light as the Means of Recognition
sanskrit:
यथालोकेन दीपस्य वकरणैभाधस्करस्य च ।
ज्ञायते वदवविभागावद तद्वच्छक्त्या वशि् वप्रये ॥ २१ ॥
transliteration:
yathā lokena dīpasya vṛkaraṇair bhāskarasya ca |
jñāyate vyavavibhāgāvat tadvat śaktyā vasi priyā || 21 ||
translation: Just as by the lamp’s light and by the rays of the sun their distinctions are known, so, beloved, by śakti the distinctionless is known.
intent_summary: Use luminous awareness itself as the means by which non-separate reality is recognized.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that just as light reveals objects, consciousness reveals reality. You do not need to go looking for the truth outside yourself; the very power of awareness can show it to you. The practice is to notice that knowing itself is already present.
scholar_explanation: The analogy of dīpa and bhāskara underscores that jñāna is self-revealing and does not require an external instrument apart from śakti. The phrase suggests a non-dual epistemology: distinctions are cognized within consciousness, while the ultimate is known through consciousness’s own power. This aligns with Pratyabhijñā and VBT’s recurring insistence that awareness is both means and goal.

speaker: Devi
title: Beyond Time, Place, and Description
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
देवदेव विशूलाङ्क कपालकृतभूषण ।
वदवदेशकालशून्या च व्यपदेशवििवजधता ॥ २२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantra |
devadeva viśūlāṅka kapālakṛtabhūṣaṇa |
vadadeśakālaśūnyā ca vyapadeśa-virjitā || 22 ||
translation: O God of gods, O trident-marked one, adorned with a skull-garland, beyond place and time and beyond all designation...
intent_summary: Praise Bhairava as beyond every conceptual coordinate, preparing the ground for direct instruction.
beginner_explanation: Devi addresses Bhairava with devotional language, then points out that he is beyond ordinary ideas like place, time, and labels. This means the truth she seeks cannot be captured by descriptions alone. She is setting up the question: how can such reality be approached directly?
scholar_explanation: This is a standard tantric gesture of stuti that simultaneously negates conceptual mapping: deśa-kāla and vyapadeśa are excluded, indicating apophatic non-duality. The iconographic epithets (viśūlāṅka, kapālakṛta-bhūṣaṇa) identify Bhairava while the negations destabilize objectification. The verse functions as a bridge from praise to inquiry in the dialogue frame.

speaker: Devi
title: How Can Bhairava Be Attained?
sanskrit:
यावस्था भवरताकारा भैरवस्योपलभ्यते ।
कैरुपायैर्मुखम् तस्य परा देवि कथं भवेत् ।
यथा सम्यगहम् देवि तथा मे ब्रूवह भैरव ॥ २३ ॥
transliteration:
yāvāsthā bhairavākārā bhairavasya upalabhyate |
kair upāyair mukham tasya parā devi kathaṃ bhavet |
yathā samyag ahaṃ devi tathā me brūhi bhairava || 23 ||
translation: In whatever state Bhairava’s form is experienced, by what means is one to approach his face? O supreme Devi, how can that be? Tell me properly, O Bhairava, as I truly am.
intent_summary: The speaker asks for the direct method by which Bhairava may be entered or realized.
beginner_explanation: Here the question is simple: if the divine can be experienced, what is the actual way in? The verse asks for a practical method, not just philosophy. It is like asking, “What do I do right now to taste this state myself?”
scholar_explanation: The key terms are upāya and mukha, suggesting means and direct access or “face” of Bhairava. The verse transitions from theological description to yogic method, anticipating the 112 dhāraṇās. In VBT logic, knowledge must become technique, and the question is precisely how non-dual presence is stabilized as lived realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Breath Rising and Falling as Source
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ऊर्ध्वे प्राणो ह्यधो जीवो विसर्गात्मा परोच्चरेत् ।
उत्पत्तिविधयस्थाने भरणाद्भवता स्थिति् ॥ २४ ॥
transliteration:
ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret |
utpattividhyavasthāne bharanād bhavataḥ sthitiḥ || 24 ||
translation: Upward is prāṇa, downward is jīva; the one whose nature is emission (visarga) moves beyond. In the station of arising and sustaining, there is your abiding through filling.
intent_summary: Attend to the upward and downward movements of life-force and rest in the sustaining point between them.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the flow of breath and life-energy. If you can notice the upward and downward movement without chasing it, there is a place of balance and stillness. The practice is to rest in that stable middle rather than following every movement.
scholar_explanation: Prāṇa and jīva are polarized as upward and downward currents, while visarga evokes the tantric cosmology of emission and return. The instruction implies a pause in the generative sequence—utpatti, vidhi, avasthāna—where bharaṇa becomes a stable abiding. This is a breath-based dhāraṇā that points to the gap between movements as the locus of śiva-śakti equilibrium.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Perceiving Bhairava in the Elements
sanskrit:
मरुतोऽन्तर्हविः वा वियद्युमावनितधनात् ।
भैरव्या भैरवस्येत्थं भैरवि व्यज्यते वपुः ॥ २५ ॥
transliteration:
maruto'ntar haviḥ vā viyad yumnāvanitadhanāt |
bhairavyā bhairavasyaitthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ || 25 ||
translation: Whether as the inner oblation of the winds or as sky, moon, woman, wealth, and the like, in this way, O Bhairavi, Bhairava’s body is manifested.
intent_summary: See the divine form disclosed through elemental and symbolic appearances in the world and body.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the divine can show up in many forms—breath, space, moonlight, and visible beauty. Instead of thinking these are separate from the sacred, you can learn to see them as expressions of one reality. The practice is a shift in seeing, not a change in the world.
scholar_explanation: The verse is polyvalent and somewhat corrupt in OCR, but its sense is that Bhairava’s vapuḥ is vyajyate through mediations such as marut, viyat, and lunar/feminine images. It invites a sacralized perception in which external and subtle forms become supports for recognition. This is not mere visualization in a narrow sense; it is a tantric re-reading of manifestation as the deity’s self-display.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Middle Beyond Motion and Rest
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न व्रजेन्न विशेच्छविमधरुद्रूपा विकावसते ।
वनविधकल्पतया मध्ये तया भैरवरूपता ॥ २६ ॥
transliteration:
na vrajed na viśec chivam adhvraudrūpa-virājate |
vana-vidhikalpatayā madhye tayā bhairavarūpatā || 26 ||
translation: One should neither go out nor enter; Śiva shines in the form of Rudra. By the imagination of the forest-like course, in the middle there is Bhairava’s form.
intent_summary: Do not move toward either outer pursuit or inner fixation; rest in the middle where Bhairava appears.
beginner_explanation: The verse tells you not to keep running outward or sinking inward. There is a middle place of balance where the mind stops splitting the world into inside and outside. In that middle, awareness can feel spacious and clear.
scholar_explanation: The injunction na vrajet na viśet rejects dual movement, while madhya becomes the pivotal locus of bhairavarūpatā. The imagery is obscure, but the practical thrust is classic VBT: the madhya between extremes is the site of non-dual revelation. The verse resonates with other gap practices in the tantra and with the centrality of madhya in later Kaula exegesis.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting at the End of the Gap
sanskrit:
कुवम्भता रेवचता िावप पूर्वता वा यदा भवेत् ।
तदन्ते शान्तनामासौ शक्त्या शान्त् प्रकाशते ॥ २७ ॥
transliteration:
kumbhitatā recakatā vāpi pūrvatā vā yadā bhavet |
tad ante śāntanāmāsau śaktyā śāntaḥ prakāśate || 27 ||
translation: When there is retention, exhalation, or the prior phase, at the end of that the one named Peace shines by śakti as peace.
intent_summary: Use the ends of breath phases as openings into peaceful, self-luminous awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse focuses on the moments when breathing changes—holding, exhaling, or just before a new breath begins. Those edge moments can become openings into stillness. The practice is to notice the quiet right at the transition and rest there.
scholar_explanation: The terms kumbhitatā and recakatā point to retention and exhalation, but the emphasis is on ante, the terminal edge of each phase. Śānta is not mere calm but a luminous condition revealed by śakti. This is a canonical sandhi practice: the junction is the doorway to dissolution of ordinary mental movement.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Subtle Flame at the Heart
sanskrit:
आमूलाविरणाभासां सूक्ष्मात् सूक्ष्मतरावत्मकाम् ।
वचन्तयेत्ताम् वद्वषट्कान्ते श्याम्यन्तीम् भैरवोदयः ॥ २८ ॥
transliteration:
āmūlāvaraṇābhāsāṃ sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatarātmakām |
vicintayettām dvādaśāntānte śāmyantīṃ bhairavodayaḥ || 28 ||
translation: One should contemplate that [power], shining from the root-covering, of nature subtler than the subtle; at the end of the twelvefold interval, as she subsides, the arising of Bhairava occurs.
intent_summary: Focus on the subtlest inner radiance at the center and let it dissolve into Bhairava-awareness.
beginner_explanation: Imagine a tiny light or warmth deep inside that gets quieter and finer as you watch it. As it fades into stillness, something larger and more spacious can appear. The instruction is to keep attention on that subtle center until it opens into stillness.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes āmūla-āvaraṇa and the dvādaśānta, a crucial yogic locus often linked to subtle breath and inner aperture. Bhairavodaya occurs when the subtle object is allowed to śāmyanti, i.e., subside into its source rather than being forcibly held. This is a visualization practice with strong tantric physiology, uniting light, center, and dissolution.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rising Through the Lightning Current
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
उद्गच्छन्तं तवडद्रूपाम् प्रवतचक्रं क्रमात्क्रमम् ।
ऊर्ध्वं मुवष्टियं याित् तािदन्ते महोदय् ॥ २९ ॥
transliteration:
udgacchantaṃ tavad-rūpam pravartacakraṃ kramāt kramam |
ūrdhvaṃ muktvā yāti tāvad ante mahodayam || 29 ||
translation: As the form rises like lightning and the wheel of movement turns step by step upward, when it is released upward, there is at the end great arising.
intent_summary: Track a rising inner current until it releases into a higher awakening.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to follow an energy or image as it rises sharply, like a flash of lightning. Do not force it; just notice the movement upward. When it naturally releases, a bigger opening or awakening can appear.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of tadit-rūpa suggests a sudden, bright ascending current, while pravarta-cakra implies cyclic movement of energetic transformation. The upshot is not to suppress motion but to let it culminate in ūrdhva release, yielding mahodayam. This resonates with ascent-oriented nāḍī and bindu contemplations in tantric yoga.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Twelvefold Cycle into Freedom
sanskrit:
क्रमद्वादशकं सम्यग् द्वादशाक्षरभेवदतम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या मुक्त्वा मुक्त्वान्तत् वशि् ॥ ३० ॥
transliteration:
krama-dvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣara-bhāvitam |
sthūla-sūkṣma-para-avasthātyā muktvā muktvāntat śivaḥ || 30 ||
translation: The twelvefold sequence, correctly contemplated as the twelve-syllabled one, having transcended the gross, subtle, and supreme states, by releasing and releasing, ends in Śiva.
intent_summary: Move through the twelvefold rhythm of practice until all levels of experience are let go into Śiva.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes a structured practice with twelve stages or a twelve-part rhythm. You move beyond ordinary experience, then beyond subtle experience, and finally beyond even spiritual concepts. The key is letting go again and again until only the deepest reality remains.
scholar_explanation: Krama-dvādaśaka and dvādaśākṣara suggest a twelvefold tantric cycle, perhaps tied to breath, phonemic sequence, or inner procession. The triple transcendence of sthūla, sūkṣma, and para mirrors standard Trika ontological layering. The repeated muktvā emphasizes progressive relinquishment culminating in identification with Śiva.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Brow-Center Ascent
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तयापूयाधशु मूर्धान्तं भङ्क्त्वा भ्रूक्षेपसेतुना ।
वनविधकल्पं मन् कृत्वा सिरूर्ध्वे सिधगोद्गम् ॥ ३१ ॥
transliteration:
tāyā pūyādhaśu mūrdhāntaṃ bhaṅktvā bhṛkṣepa-setunā |
vanavidhakalpaṃ man kṛtvā sirūrdhve sidhagodgam || 31 ||
translation: Having broken through to the top of the head by the bridge of a glance upward at the brow, and making the mind like a thought-free forest, one rises into the upper channel and attains perfection.
intent_summary: Use an upward turn of attention to pierce the crown and let the mind expand beyond ordinary thought.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to gently lift your attention upward, as if looking toward the space above your eyebrows and then beyond the top of your head. The mind is then made quiet and spacious, like a forest with no one walking through it. In that openness, a deeper state can appear.
scholar_explanation: The practice uses bhṛkṣepa, a subtle upward gaze or eyebrow-lift, as a bridge (setu) to break through the mūrdhānta, the crown region. By making the mind vanish into a vana-vat, forest-like expanse, awareness moves into the upper channel (sīrūrdhva / suṣumṇā imagery) toward siddhi or direct realization. This is a classic subtle-body ascent technique aligned with kuṇḍalinī- and suṣumṇā-based contemplations.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fivefold Void Meditation
sanskrit:
वशवखपक्षैवश्चिरूपैमण्डलै् शून्यपञ्चकम् ।
ध्यायतोऽनुत्तरे शून्ये प्रिेशो हृदये भवेत् ॥ ३२ ॥
transliteration:
vaśa-vakha-pakṣaivaś cirūpai maṇḍalaiḥ śūnya-pañcakam |
dhyāyato'nuttare śūnye prīśo hṛdaye bhavet || 32 ||
translation: Meditating on the five voids through the forms of the controlled directions and wing-like circles, entry into the supreme void arises in the heart.
intent_summary: Contemplate the subtle voids until the heart opens into the unsurpassed inner emptiness.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests focusing on spaciousness in several directions, almost like sensing empty circles or openings around you. Instead of chasing thoughts, you rest in the feeling of inner space. That spaciousness can then be felt not just around you but in the heart itself.
scholar_explanation: The pañca-śūnya, five voids, are contemplated through maṇḍala-like formations and directional expansions, suggesting a spatialized interiorization of awareness. The result is entry into anuttara-śūnya, the supreme void, with hṛdaya as the locus of recognition rather than mere blankness. This is not nihilistic emptiness but a luminous śūnya tied to Trika hṛdaya doctrine.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorption in the Supreme Void
sanskrit:
ईदृशेन क्रमेणैि यि कुिावप वचन्तना ।
शून्ये कुड्ये परे पािे स्वयम् लीना िरप्रदा ॥ ३३ ॥
transliteration:
īdṛśena krameṇaiva yai kutrāpi vicintanā |
śūnye kuḍye pare pāre svayam līnā vara-pradā || 33 ||
translation: By this method, whatever one contemplates anywhere becomes self-absorbed into the void, the wall, and the transcendent beyond; this grants the supreme boon.
intent_summary: Let any thought or object dissolve by seeing it as empty and absorbed into the transcendent beyond.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that if you use this way of contemplating, anything you think about can melt back into emptiness. It is like watching an image dissolve into a blank wall or into open space. The result is a deeper freedom, because your mind stops clinging to what it sees.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes a generalized śūnya-bhāvanā in which any vicāra or visualization becomes līna, absorbed, into śūnya, kuḍya, and pare pāra—the empty, the wall-like, and the transcendence beyond. The teaching is that phenomena are not denied but recognized as dissolving presentations of consciousness. This yields vara-pradā, the supreme boon, i.e., recognition of the Self as the background of all appearances.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gaze into the Crown Void
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कपालान्तमधनो न्यस्य वतष्ठन्मीवलतलोचन् ।
क्रमेण मनसो दार्ढ्यात् लक्षयेत् लक्ष्यं उत्तमम् ॥ ३४ ॥
transliteration:
kapālāntam adhono nyasya tiṣṭhan mīlitalocanaḥ |
krameṇa manaso dārḍhyāt lakṣayet lakṣyam uttamam || 34 ||
translation: Placing the lower part of the skull beneath and remaining with closed eyes, one should gradually, through the firmness of mind, direct attention to the supreme aim.
intent_summary: Stabilize the mind and inwardly aim at the highest reality while keeping the body still and the eyes closed.
beginner_explanation: Here the practice is very simple: sit quietly, close your eyes, and keep your attention steady. Instead of letting the mind wander, aim it toward the deepest possible sense of presence. With patience, that steady attention itself becomes the path.
scholar_explanation: The verse emphasizes dārḍhya, firmness of mind, while the gaze is withdrawn (mīlita-locana) and the head/skull posture is subtly arranged. Lakṣya here is not a worldly object but the uttama-lakṣya, the supreme aim, often read as pure consciousness or Bhairava-awareness. This is an inward concentration practice in which bodily steadiness supports one-pointed recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Suṣumnā Heart-Light
sanskrit:
मध्यनाडी मध्यसंस्था विससूत्राभरूपया ।
ध्यातान्तव्योमया देव्या तया देवि प्रकाशते ॥ ३५ ॥
transliteration:
madhya-nāḍī madhya-saṃsthā viśva-sūtrābha-rūpayā |
dhyātāntar-vyomayā devyā tayā devī prakāśate || 35 ||
translation: The middle channel, abiding in the center and resembling the thread of the universe, is the inner sky; by meditating on that goddess, O Devī, she shines forth.
intent_summary: Meditate on the central channel as the inner sky so that the goddess of awareness becomes manifest.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the middle energy channel in the body, imagined as a thread running through everything. When you focus on that central line, it can feel like an inner open sky. In that spacious center, awareness shines more clearly.
scholar_explanation: Madhya-nāḍī refers to suṣumṇā, the central channel, described as viśva-sūtra, the thread supporting the cosmos, and as antar-vyoma, the inner space. The verse identifies that centrality with Devī herself, indicating that the śakti-path is the locus of prakāśa. This aligns with Trika’s view that the middle axis is not merely anatomical but a direct icon of consciousness as luminous openness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Brow-Closed Gaze at the Bindu
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कररुद्धदृगस्त्रेण भ्रूभेदाद्द्वाररोधनात् ।
दृष्टे विन्दौ क्रमाल्लीने तन्मध्ये परमा वस्थवत् ॥ ३६ ॥
transliteration:
kara-ruddha-dṛgastreṇa bhru-bhedād dvāra-rodhanāt |
dṛṣṭe bindau kramāl līne tan-madhye paramāvasthitiḥ || 36 ||
translation: By the weapon of vision restrained by the hand, by closing the gate through piercing the brow, when the bindu is seen and gradually dissolved, there is the supreme state in its midst.
intent_summary: Seal the senses, focus at the brow, and let the subtle point dissolve into the highest state.
beginner_explanation: This verse describes blocking outward distractions and looking inward at a tiny point of light or attention. As that point becomes clearer, you do not hold onto it forever; you let it soften and disappear. In the middle of that fading, a deeper stillness appears.
scholar_explanation: The kara-ruddha-dṛg-astra suggests shielding or restraining the gaze, while bhru-bheda indicates penetration at the brow gate. The bindu is then observed and allowed to merge (līna), revealing paramāvasthiti, the supreme abiding state. This is a refined trataka-like inner focus transformed into laya, where the point serves as a doorway to nondual stillness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bindu Dissolution at the Heart
sanskrit:
धामान्त् क्षोभसम्भूतसूक्ष्माविवतलकाकृवतम् ।
विन्दुं वशखान्ते हृदये लयान्ते ध्यायतो लय् ॥ ३७ ॥
transliteration:
dhāmāntāḥ kṣobha-sambhūta-sūkṣmāviṭa-lakākṛtim |
binduṃ śaśākhānte hṛdaye layānte dhyāyato layaḥ || 37 ||
translation: Meditating, at the end of the heart and at the end of the moon-disk, on the bindu as a subtle form born from inner agitation, dissolution is attained.
intent_summary: Contemplate the subtle bindu until it dissolves into heart-centered absorption.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a tiny inner focal point that appears from subtle movement in awareness. You keep your attention on it at the heart, or at a luminous inner spot, until it naturally dissolves. When it dissolves, the mind sinks into quiet absorption.
scholar_explanation: The bindu here is linked with dhāma and kṣobha, subtle pulsation or disturbance arising within the luminous field, and the practice ends in laya at the hṛdaya. References to śaśāṅka/śaśākhānta suggest a cool lunar locus, often associated with refined inner nectar or inner radiance. The verse teaches that even the subtlest object of contemplation is to be absorbed, not grasped, so that laya becomes realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Sound into Brahman
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अनाहते पािकणेऽभिशब्दे सवरद्द्रुते ।
शब्दब्रह्मवण वनष्णात् परं ब्रह्मावधगच्छवत ॥ ३८ ॥
transliteration:
anāhate pāṇikahne'bhīśabde svarad-drute |
śabda-brahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati || 38 ||
translation: By immersion in the unstruck sound within the palm-like cavity, and in the swift flow of inner sound, one becomes adept in sound-Brahman and attains the supreme Brahman.
intent_summary: Attend to the subtle unstruck inner sound until it carries the mind beyond sound into the highest reality.
beginner_explanation: Listen inwardly for a sound that is not coming from outside, like a soft ringing or hum in stillness. Don’t try to create it; just notice it and stay with it. As your attention deepens, the sound itself can lead you into a quieter, more spacious awareness.
scholar_explanation: Anāhata, the unstruck sound, is the classic nāda of inner audibility, here coupled with the rapid movement of svara-druti. Mastery in śabda-brahman leads beyond sonic phenomena to para-brahman, showing the Tantric use of sound as a ladder that is ultimately transcended. The practice rests in subtle audition until awareness recognizes itself as the source of the vibration.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Void Beyond Breath
sanskrit:
प्रणिावदसमुच्चारात् प्लुतान्ते शून्यभािानात् ।
शून्यया परया शक्त्या शून्यतामेवत भैरवि ॥ ३९ ॥
transliteration:
praṇavādi-samuccārāt plutānte śūnyabhāvanāt |
śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi || 39 ||
translation: Through the utterance of pranava and other mantras, and by contemplating voidness at the end of the prolonged sound, Bhairavi reaches emptiness by the supreme शक्ति of emptiness.
intent_summary: Use mantra and the pause after it to enter the void through breath and sound suspension.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when you chant a sacred sound and then let it end and become still, there is a quiet gap you can enter. Rather than rushing to the next breath or thought, rest in that opening. That stillness is described as the doorway to emptiness.
scholar_explanation: The verse combines praṇava-japa with pluta, the prolonged mantra ending, followed by śūnya-bhāvanā. The śūnyā śakti is not mere negation but the dynamic power of opening that reveals śūnyatā as the nature of consciousness. This is one of the clearest examples of using sonic cadence and pause as a direct route into nonconceptual awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Form Dissolves into Emptiness
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्यावप िणधस्य पूिाधन्तािनुभाियेत् ।
शून्यया शून्यभूतोऽसौ शून्याकार् पुमान्भवेत् ॥ ४० ॥
transliteration:
yasya kasyāpi varṇasya pūrvāntāv anubhāvayet |
śūnyayā śūnyabhūto'sau śūnyākāraḥ pumān bhavet || 40 ||
translation: Whatever sound or letter one may contemplate, if one experiences its beginning and end, by emptiness that person becomes empty and takes on the form of emptiness.
intent_summary: Trace any sound or form from start to finish until it dissolves into empty awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to notice how anything begins and ends, whether it is a sound, a thought, or an image. If you keep following it without clinging, it naturally disappears. What remains is a spacious, open kind of presence.
scholar_explanation: By observing the pūrvānta and antya, the beginning and end of any varṇa or perceptible object, the practitioner enters śūnya-bhāva. The result is śūnyabhūta and śūnyākāra, an identification not with a thing but with the formless openness that underlies all formation. This is a generalized contemplative dissolution technique bridging mantra, perception, and ontological emptiness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Continuous Inner Sound Meditation
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तन्त्र्यावदिाद्यशब्देषु दीघेषु क्रमसवम्स्थते् ।
अनन्यचेता् प्रत्यन्ते परव्योमिपुभधिेत् ॥ ४१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
tantryāvaḍiādyaśabdeṣu dīrghesu kramasavasthate |
ananyacetāḥ pratyante paravyomipu bhadhet || 41 ||
translation: In the long, continuous sounds beginning with the stringed instrument’s tone and other sounds, with one-pointed mind, one should attend to the supreme ether at the end.
intent_summary: Use sustained listening to outer or inner sound as a doorway into the limitless awareness beyond sound.
beginner_explanation: Listen carefully to a long, continuous sound, like the hum of an instrument or a sustained tone. As the sound keeps going, place your attention on the quiet awareness that notices it, especially at the point where the sound fades. This turns listening into a way of becoming calm and spacious inside.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses the extended continuity of śabda as a support for ananyacetas, a mind without division. The practitioner attends to the paravyoman, the supreme/inner expanse revealed at the termination of audible vibration, where sound resolves into awareness. It belongs to the VBT’s sound-based methods that convert sensory continuity into recognition of the background consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mantra Dissolution into Silence
sanskrit:
वपण्डमन्त्रस्य सिधस्य स्थूलिणधक्रमेण तु ।
अधेन्दुविन्दुनादान्त् शून्योच्चाराद्भिेवच्छि् ॥ ४२ ॥
transliteration:
piṇḍamantrasya sidhasya sthūliṇadhakrameṇa tu |
adhendu vindu nādāntāt śūnyoccārādbhivecchit || 42 ||
translation: For the perfected embodied mantra, by the क्रम of gross articulation, from half-moon, bindu, and nāda up to the end, one should dissolve into the utterance of emptiness.
intent_summary: Trace mantra from articulated sound back into subtler stages until it disappears into silence and emptiness.
beginner_explanation: Take a mantra and notice how it changes from a spoken sound into subtler and subtler levels. First hear the clearer parts, then the faint inner point, then the ringing tone, and finally the silence behind it. The practice is to follow the mantra inward until only stillness remains.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes the siddha piṇḍamantra as moving through gross utterance toward the subtle sequence of ardha-candra, bindu, and nāda, culminating in śūnya-uccāra, an utterance that is really silence. This is a classic Tantric internalization of mantra, where phonemic articulation is re-seen as a contraction and reabsorption of śakti. The goal is not mere suppression of speech but recognition of the śūnyatā that underlies mantra resonance.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Body as Ether
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वनजदेहे सिधवदक्कम् युगपद्भाियेवद्वयत् ।
वनविधकल्पमनास्तस्य वियत्सिधम् प्रितधते ॥ ४३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
nija dehe siddhavad vatkaṃ yugapad bhāvayen dvayāt |
nivikalpa manas tasya viyatsiddhaṃ pravartate || 43 ||
translation: In one’s own body, as if it were already perfected and simultaneously nondual, one should contemplate it. For that person whose mind is free of conceptual construction, the perfection of the ether arises.
intent_summary: Contemplate the body as already perfected and spacious so that the mind settles into open, non-conceptual awareness.
beginner_explanation: Instead of seeing your body as a problem to fix, imagine it as already whole and complete. Let your attention rest on the feeling of being here, without dividing yourself into parts or judging them. When you do this, your mind can become very open and spacious.
scholar_explanation: Here the body is approached as siddhavat, as though already accomplished, and bhāvana is used to collapse dvaya, dualistic splitting. When vikalpa ceases, viyat-siddhi emerges: the realization of the body as space-like, echoing Śaiva embodiment where the limited body is recognized as a manifestation of cit-ākāśa. This dhāraṇā resonates with the VBT’s repeated move from form to expanse.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rear and Root Void
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यम् मूलशून्यम् युगपद्भाियेच्च य् ।
शरीरवनरपेवक्षण्या शक्त्या शून्यमना भवेत् ॥ ४४ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ yugapad bhāvayecca yaḥ |
śarīra nirapekṣiṇyā śaktyā śūnyamano bhavet || 44 ||
translation: One who contemplates at once the void of the back and the void of the root becomes of empty mind through the power that is independent of the body.
intent_summary: Expand awareness into the body’s back and base while letting the mind empty into a nonphysical power.
beginner_explanation: Feel the space behind your back and the space at the base of your body at the same time. Do not tighten around sensations; just let them be open and roomy. This can make the mind feel less crowded and more still.
scholar_explanation: The verse pairs pṛṣṭaśūnya and mūlaśūnya, two loci of emptiness that bracket embodied awareness. Śakti is described as śarīra-nirapekṣiṇī, independent of the body, indicating that the real subtle power is not reducible to somatic form. The result is śūnya-manas, an emptied mind that remains alert rather than inert.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Heart and Root Void
sanskrit:
पृष्टशून्यं मूलशून्यं हृच्छून्यं भाियेविरम् ।
युगपवन्नविधकल्पत्वावन्नविधकल्पोदयस्तत् ॥ ४५ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ hṛcchūnyaṃ bhāvayed dhṛvam |
yugapannivikalpatvānnivikalpodayastataḥ || 45 ||
translation: One should firmly contemplate the void of the back, the void of the root, and the void of the heart. Because of simultaneous non-conceptuality, there arises the dawning of non-conceptual awareness.
intent_summary: Hold several inner centers as empty at once until thought drops away and naked awareness shines forth.
beginner_explanation: Bring attention to the back, the base, and the heart, and imagine them as open spaces. Try to feel all three at once without naming or analyzing them. When the mind stops dividing experience, a very clear and quiet awareness can appear.
scholar_explanation: This verse deepens the previous one by adding hṛcchūnya, the void of the heart-center, to the embodied triad. The simultaneous contemplation produces yugapad-nivikalpatva, a non-sequential suspension of conceptualizing activity, from which nivikalpa उदय, the arising of nonconceptuality, occurs. It is a dhāraṇā of distributed interior emptiness leading to immediate recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Brief Body-Field Emptiness
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
तनूदेशे शून्यतैि क्षणमािं विभाियेत् ।
वनविधकल्पं वनविधकल्पो वनविधकल्पस्वरूपभाक् ॥ ४६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
tanūdeśe śūnyatāiva kṣaṇamātraṃ vibhāvayet |
nivikalpaṃ nivikalpo nivikalpasvarūpabhāk || 46 ||
translation: In the region of the body, one should contemplate emptiness for just a moment. Becoming non-conceptual, one becomes one whose nature is non-conceptual awareness.
intent_summary: Use a brief flash of attention on bodily emptiness to trigger a stable non-conceptual state.
beginner_explanation: For just an instant, feel the body as empty space rather than as a solid object. Even a very short glimpse can interrupt overthinking. The idea is that a moment of openness can reveal a deeper stillness.
scholar_explanation: The VBT often emphasizes instantaneous recognition; here a kṣaṇamātra contemplation of śūnyatā in the tanūdeśa is enough. The repetition of nivikalpa underscores a shift from doing to being, where the practitioner is no longer merely devoid of concepts but 'possesses' the very form of non-conceptual awareness. This is a concise instruction in immediate interiorization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Body Filled with Sky
sanskrit:
सिं देहगतं द्रव्यं वियद्व्याप्तं मृगेक्षणे ।
विभाियेत्ततस्तस्य भावना सा वस्थरा भवेत् ॥ ४७ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ dehagataṃ dravyaṃ viyadvyāptaṃ mṛgekṣaṇe |
vibhāvayet tataḥ tasya bhāvanā sā sthirā bhavet || 47 ||
translation: O doe-eyed one, one should contemplate all substances in the body as pervaded by space. Then that contemplation becomes steady.
intent_summary: See all bodily matter as permeated by space until that perception becomes stable and continuous.
beginner_explanation: Imagine that every part of your body is filled with open space. Instead of feeling dense and closed, your body can be felt as airy and spacious. Repeating this gently makes the feeling more steady.
scholar_explanation: The body’s contents, sarvaṃ dehagataṃ dravyam, are visualized as viyadvyāpta, permeated by ākāśa/viyat. The instruction to vibhāvayet indicates deliberate contemplative imaging that, through repetition, stabilizes as bhāvanā. This is a classic śākta-śaiva transformation of materiality into spatiality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Indivisibility Contemplation
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
देहान्तरे त्ववविभागम् वभवत्तभूतम् विवचन्तयेत् ।
न वकंवचदन्तरे तस्य ध्यायन्नध्येयभाग्भवेत् ॥ ४८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
dehāntare tv avibhāgaṃ bhāvitaṃ bhūtam vicintayet |
na kiṃcid antare tasya dhyāyann adhyeyabhāg bhavet || 48 ||
translation: Within the body, one should contemplate the undivided, existing reality. Meditating that there is nothing within it, one becomes a participant in the meditated object.
intent_summary: Contemplate inner reality as undivided emptiness so that subject and object collapse into one field.
beginner_explanation: Look inside and do not find separate pieces or a solid center—just one open continuity. Then keep resting with the sense that there is nothing to grasp inside. As the split between observer and observed weakens, meditation becomes more intimate and direct.
scholar_explanation: Avibhāga, undividedness, is the key term: within dehāntara one contemplates the bhūta/being as a seamless whole. The claim that 'nothing' is inside (na kiṃcid antare) functions to undo objectification, and the meditator becomes adhyeyabhāk, sharing in the nature of the object of meditation. This is a strong nondual instruction, moving from spatial imagery to the collapse of relational duality.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Heart Sky Absorption
sanskrit:
हृद्याकाशे वनलीनाक्ष् पिसम्पुटमध्यग् ।
अनन्यचेता् सुभगे परं सौभावयमाप्नुयात् ॥ ४९ ॥
transliteration:
hṛdy ākāśe nilīnāṅgaḥ padasaṃpuṭa madhyagaḥ |
ananyacetāḥ subhage paraṃ saubhāgyam āpnuyāt || 49 ||
translation: With limbs absorbed in the heart-space and situated in the middle of the closed posture of the feet, one whose mind is one-pointed, O beautiful one, attains supreme good fortune.
intent_summary: Gather the body into the heart-space and remain wholly absorbed there to awaken a profound blessedness.
beginner_explanation: Bring your attention into the heart area and let the rest of the body feel gathered there. Stay very still and focused, as if everything is collecting into one inner center. This can give a feeling of peace, fullness, and deep well-being.
scholar_explanation: The image is of limbs nilīnāṅga, absorbed, in hṛd-ākāśa, the heart-space or cit-ākāśa. The posture detail (padasaṃpuṭa-madhyaga) supports embodied concentration, while ananyacetāḥ indicates exclusive, undivided attention. The result is saubhāgya in the Tantric sense: auspiciousness and fortunate alignment with the heart’s space-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Twelve-Finger Threshold
sanskrit:
सिधत् स्वशरीरस्य द्वादशान्ते मनोलयात् ।
दृढिुद्धेदृधढीभूतं तत्त्वलक्ष्यं प्रितधते ॥ ५० ॥
transliteration:
siddheṣu svaśarīrasya dvādaśānte manolayāt |
dṛḍhībhūte dṛḍhībhūtaṃ tattvalakṣyaṃ pravartate || 50 ||
translation: In the perfected body, through the dissolution of mind at the twelve-finger point of one’s own body, the fixed, fully established goal of reality becomes manifest.
intent_summary: Let the mind dissolve at the subtle twelve-finger locus so that reality itself becomes directly apparent.
beginner_explanation: Focus on a subtle point just beyond the body, often described as a little distance from the center or head. As attention becomes very still there, thoughts can quiet down on their own. In that stillness, the deepest truth is said to become obvious.
scholar_explanation: The dvādaśānta is the classic subtle locus beyond the body where prāṇa and mind can resolve. Manolaya here does not mean unconsciousness but a refined settling of mentation into tattva-lakṣya, the target of reality or principle. The verse links embodied subtle anatomy with the culminating recognition of the accomplished state (siddha-deha).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attention at the Twelve-Finger Point
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यथा तथा यि ति द्वादशान्ते मन् वक्षपेत् ॥
प्रवतक्षणम् क्षीणिृत्तेिैलक्षण्यं वदनैभधिेत् ॥ ५१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
yathā tathā yi ti dvādaśānte man vakṣapet ||
pravata-kṣaṇam kṣīṇi-vṛttei-lailakṣaṇyaṃ vadanairbhadhiet || 51 ||
translation:
Vijñānabhairava Tantra.
However and in whatever way the mind may be projected toward the dvādaśānta, at that instant, when mental activity has become thin, the distinctiveness of the face or the manifested field dissolves. || 51 ||
intent_summary: Use attention at the dvādaśānta, the subtle point associated with the breath and crown, to let mental activity thin out and reveal a non-different awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a subtle place called the dvādaśānta, a point “twelve finger-widths” from the body, often linked with the breath's endpoint. The practice is to place attention there and let the mind become quiet on its own. When that happens, the usual sense of separation softens.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā uses the dvādaśānta as a liminal locus of prāṇa and consciousness, a classic Śaiva contemplative pivot. As vṛtti becomes kṣīṇa, the manifest distinctions of vadanādi-lakṣaṇya are absorbed, disclosing a non-dual mode of awareness. This aligns with VBT methods that exploit subtle spatial thresholds rather than discursive meditation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Burnt City Contemplation
sanskrit:
कालाविना कालपदादुवत्थतेन स्वकं पुरम् ।
प्लुष्टं विवचन्तयेदन्ते शान्ताभासस्तदा भवेत् ॥ ५२ ॥
transliteration:
kālāvinā kālapadādutthitena svakaṃ puram |
pluṣṭaṃ vivacintayedante śāntābhāsas tadā bhavet || 52 ||
translation: One should contemplate one’s own body-city, arisen from the station of time and consumed by fire, and at the end there arises a semblance of peace. || 52 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate the body and world as already burned through by time so the mind releases its grasp and a शांताभास, a peaceful luminosity, appears.
beginner_explanation: Here the body is imagined as a city that time has already burned down. This is not meant to depress you, but to loosen your attachment to the body and worldly identity. When that grip relaxes, a quiet, peaceful clarity can shine through.
scholar_explanation: The verse deploys śmaśāna-like imagery: kāla consumes svakaṃ puraṃ, the embodied microcosm, revealing śāntābhāsa, a peaceful appearance or residue beyond fear. Such contemplations function as disenchantment (vairāgya) and disidentification, preparing the mind for absorption. The emphasis is not nihilism but a phenomenological turn from form to the luminous witness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Dual and Nondual
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एवं एव जगत्सं द्विधं ध्यात्वा विकल्पतः ।
अनन्यचेतस् पुम्स् पुम्भाव् परमो भवेत् ॥ ५३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
evaṃ eva jagatsaṃ dvिधaṃ dhyātvā vikalpataḥ |
ananyacetas pumस् pumbhāv paramo bhavet || 53 ||
translation:
Vijñānabhairava Tantra.
Thus, contemplating the world as divided in a twofold way through conceptualization, one whose mind is no longer directed elsewhere becomes the supreme state of manhood or full being. || 53 ||
intent_summary: Use reflective seeing of the world's dual appearance, then let the mind become single-pointed and beyond division.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to look carefully at how the world appears split into opposites and separate things. Then, instead of chasing those differences, let your attention settle into one steady presence. That steady presence is said to be the highest human fulfillment.
scholar_explanation: The instruction begins from vikalpa, conceptual bifurcation, and redirects it toward ananyacetas, an undistracted mind. Pumbhāva here signals पूर्णता or mature subjectivity, not merely gender; it indicates the realization of one’s fullest mode beyond fragmented cognition. The verse turns dualistic perception into a gate for recognition of unity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolving Subtle Tattvas
sanskrit:
स्वदेहे जगतो वापि सूक्ष्मसूक्ष्मतराणि च ।
तत्त्वानि यानि विलयं ध्यात्वान्ते व्यज्यते परा ॥ ५४ ॥
transliteration:
svadehe jagato vāpi sūkṣma-sūkṣmatarāṇi ca |
tattvāni yāni vilayaṃ dhyātvānte vyajyate parā || 54 ||
translation: In one’s own body, or also in the world, whatever subtle and subtler principles there are—by meditating on their dissolution, in the end the supreme is revealed. || 54 ||
intent_summary: Contemplate all subtle constituents of body and world as dissolving, so the supreme reality can emerge.
beginner_explanation: This verse says to notice everything that makes up you and the world, down to the most subtle levels, and imagine it all dissolving. As the pieces fade, what remains is not emptiness in a dead sense but a higher reality. It is like letting a picture dissolve so the screen becomes visible.
scholar_explanation: The verse targets sūkṣma and sūkṣmatara tattvas, inviting laya of all ontic layers within deha and jagat. The result is vyajyate parā, the manifestation of Parā-śakti/Paramaśiva as the substratum of all categories. This is a contemplative deconstruction of tattvic multiplicity into non-dual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Heart from the Twelve-Finger Field
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
पीनां च दुिधलां शविं ध्यात्वा द्वादशगोचरे ।
प्रविश्य हृदये ध्यायन्मुि् स्वातन्त्र्यमाप्नुयात् ॥ ५५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
pīnāṃ ca dudhilāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagocare |
praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktiṃ svātantryam āpnuyāt || 55 ||
translation:
Vijñānabhairava Tantra.
Having contemplated the dense, dual power in the field of the twelve, and entering the heart, one should meditate and attain liberation, freedom. || 55 ||
intent_summary: Focus on the energetic field of the dvādaśa and then inwardly enter the heart to realize freedom.
beginner_explanation: The verse suggests that there is a powerful current or energy in the subtle twelvefold field. You first notice that power, then turn inward to the heart center and rest there. The result is freedom, not because something new is added, but because your attention returns to its source.
scholar_explanation: The phrase dvādaśagocare indicates the subtle domain around the dvādaśānta/inner periphery, while hṛdaya denotes the central Śaiva locus of consciousness. The verse couples a concentrated visualization of śakti with inward entry, culminating in svātantrya, a key Trika term for divine freedom. Liberation here is not elsewhere but disclosed in the heart as the source of all movement.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Cosmic Pathways
sanskrit:
भुिनार्ध्वावदरूपेण वचन्तयेत्क्रमशोऽवखलम् ।
स्थूलसूक्ष्मपरवस्थत्या यािदन्ते मनोलय् ॥ ५६ ॥
transliteration:
bhuvibārthāvavadharūpeṇa cintayet kramaśo'khilam |
sthūla-sūkṣma-parāvasthatyā yāvadante manolayaḥ || 56 ||
translation: One should gradually contemplate the whole in the form of the cosmic pathways, until by the condition of gross, subtle, and supreme states the mind is finally dissolved. || 56 ||
intent_summary: Use a graduated visualization of the cosmos and its levels of reality to carry the mind into dissolution.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to picture reality as a structured path or pattern, step by step. You look at the gross, the subtle, and the highest level, without rushing. As your attention becomes absorbed in this wider order, the thinking mind naturally quiets and dissolves.
scholar_explanation: The practice evokes bhuvanādhva and its ordered traversal, contemplating the whole in krama across sthūla, sūkṣma, and parā states. Such layered vision organizes perception into a transpersonal cosmogram that culminates in manolaya. It is a classic Tantric use of macrocosmic structure to dissolve ordinary cognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Tracing Reality by the Cosmic Path
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अस्य सिधस्य विश्वस्य पयधन्तेषु समन्तत् ।
अर्ध्वप्रवक्रयया तत्त्वं शैिं ध्यत्वा महोदय् ॥ ५७ ॥
transliteration:
asya siddhasya viśvasya paryanteṣu samantataḥ |
adhvaprakriyayā tattvaṃ śaivaṃ dhyātvā mahodayam || 57 ||
translation: Within the perfected universe, all around its limits, by the method of the path one should meditate on the Śaiva principle, and then there is great awakening. || 57 ||
intent_summary: Trace the universe’s cosmic structure all around its bounds and meditate on the Śaiva principle until a great awakening arises.
beginner_explanation: The verse invites you to imagine the universe as a complete, perfected field with edges and pathways. By contemplating this whole pattern, you gradually sense the deeper principle that holds it all together. That recognition brings a big inner waking-up.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā extends adhva-prakriyā to the paryanta of the siddha viśva, reading the cosmos as a complete Śaiva map. Meditating on tattvaṃ śaivam reveals that all pathways culminate in Mahodaya, the great arising or exaltation of recognition. It harmonizes cosmology with soteriology: the world’s structure itself becomes the means of awakening.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The World as Empty Space
sanskrit:
विश्वमेतन्महादेवि शून्यभूतं विवचन्तयेत् ।
तिैि च मनो लीनं ततस्तल्लयभाजनम् ॥ ५८ ॥
transliteration:
viśvam etan mahādevi śūnyabhūtaṃ vicintayet |
tatraiva ca mano līnaṃ tatas tallayabhājanam || 58 ||
translation: O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this universe as become empty. There, the mind becomes absorbed, and then one becomes a vessel of that dissolution. || 58 ||
intent_summary: See the entire universe as empty so the mind merges into that emptiness and becomes fit for dissolution.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to look at the whole world as if it were empty space. When you do that, the mind has nothing solid to hold onto and settles down. In that stillness, you become more open to a deep merging beyond ordinary thought.
scholar_explanation: The key move is śūnyabhūtaṃ vicintayet: the universe is contemplated as emptied of fixed essence, not denied. Mano līnaṃ marks absorption into that śūnya field, and the practitioner becomes tallayabhājana, a receptacle for laya. This is a central VBT void-practice linking emptiness with conscious absorption rather than mere negation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing Through the Empty Vessel
sanskrit:
घटावदभाजने दृवष्टं वभवत्तस्त्यक्त्वा विवनवक्षपेत् ।
तल्लयं तत्क्षणाद्गत्वा तल्लयात्तन्मयो भवेत् ॥ ५९ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādibhājane dṛṣṭiṃ bhittvā tyaktvā vinikṣipet |
tallayaṃ tatkṣaṇād gatvā tallayāt tanmayo bhavet || 59 ||
translation: Having broken the gaze that rests in a pot or vessel and having cast it beyond, one should let it fall there; by reaching that dissolution instantly, one becomes identified with that dissolution. || 59 ||
intent_summary: Break fixation on bounded forms and throw the gaze into the open so awareness becomes one with dissolution itself.
beginner_explanation: Think of staring at the inside of a pot: the verse says to break that habit of looking at things as solid containers. Let your attention fall beyond the object, into open space. When the mind lands there, it can merge with that openness.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses ghaṭa-bhājana imagery to undo container-bound perception, a standard Tantric critique of object fixation. By vinikṣepa of dṛṣṭi beyond the form, the practitioner enters laya and becomes tanmaya with that state. It is a precise technique of de-objectifying perception through spatial deferral.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gaze into the Chosen Void
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वनिृधक्षवगवरवभत्त्यावददेशे दृवष्टं विवनवक्षपेत् ।
विलीने मानसे भावे िृत्तिक्षीण् प्रजायते ॥ ६० ॥
transliteration:
niruddha-śikharāvalambitād deśe dṛṣṭiṃ vinikṣipet |
vilīne mānase bhāve vṛttikṣīṇaṃ prajāyate || 60 ||
translation: One should cast the gaze into a place supported by a restrained peak or summit; when the mental state has dissolved, the fluctuations become exhausted. || 60 ||
intent_summary: Place attention in a fixed open location so the mind-state dissolves and mental fluctuations wear out.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests resting your gaze on a still point, like the top of a mountain or a quiet peak. By holding attention there, the mind gradually becomes less busy. When the inner image dissolves, thoughts lose their fuel.
scholar_explanation: The phrase niruddha-śikharāvalambita points to a stabilized focal summit, a contemplative apex where dṛṣṭi is placed. As mānasa-bhāva vilīna, vṛttis are exhausted, showing the VBT method of using spatial concentration to induce psychical laya. This stands close to ādhāra-based dhāraṇās in later verses.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Middle Between Two Thoughts
sanskrit:
उभयोभाधियोज्ञाधने ध्यात्वा मध्यं समाश्रयेत् ।
युगपच्च द्वयं त्यक्त्वा मध्ये तत्त्वं प्रकाशते ॥ ६१ ॥
transliteration:
ubhayobhādhiyojñādhane dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet |
yugapacca dvayaṃ tyaktvā madhye tattvaṃ prakāśate || 61 ||
translation: Having meditated on the middle place between the two, one should take refuge in the middle. By abandoning both at once, the truth shines in the middle.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to rest in the gap or center between opposites, where true reality becomes evident.
beginner_explanation: Notice the small pause between two thoughts, two breaths, or two impulses. Instead of following either side, rest in that in-between stillness. In that quiet center, awareness becomes clear by itself.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic madhya-dṛṣṭi dhāraṇā: the practitioner contemplates the interval (madhya) between dual poles and then relinquishes both simultaneously, allowing tattva to manifest. The verse points to non-conceptual awareness arising when polarities are not held as separate. It resonates with VBT passages on the gap between breaths and between perceptions as a doorway to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abandoning Mental Objects
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भावे त्यक्ते निरुद्धा चित्तं नैव भावान्तरं व्रजेत् ।
तदा तन्मध्यभावेन विकसत्यतिभावना ॥ ६२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
bhāve tyakte niruddhaṃ cittaṃ naiva bhāvāntaraṃ vrajet |
tadā tanmadhyabhāvena vikasatyatibhāvanā || 62 ||
translation: When an object of thought has been abandoned and the mind is restrained, it should not move to another object. Then, by that middle condition, supreme contemplation blossoms.
intent_summary: The verse teaches stopping the mind from jumping to a new object after dropping the previous one, so a deeper contemplation can emerge.
beginner_explanation: Usually when one thought ends, another quickly takes its place. Here the instruction is to let go of the first thought and not replace it immediately. In that pause, a deeper stillness can open like a flower.
scholar_explanation: The dhāraṇā emphasizes bhāva-tyāga and citta-nirodha without substitution, so the mind does not migrate to bhāvāntara. The ensuing state, tanmadhyabhāva, is the fertile interval in which atibhāvanā—an intensified contemplative realization—unfolds spontaneously. This reflects the VBT strategy of interrupting conceptual continuity to reveal the self-luminous ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The World as Conscious Body
sanskrit:
सिं देहं चिन्मयं हि जगद्वा परिभावयेत् ।
युगपन्निविधकल्पेन मनसा परमोदयः ॥ ६३ ॥
transliteration:
sīṃ dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagadvā paribhāvayet |
yugapannividhaकल्पena manasa paramaodayaḥ || 63 ||
translation: One should imagine that the body is made of consciousness, or that the world is [made of consciousness]. Through a mind held in twofold-but-simultaneous कल्पना (imagination/conception), supreme awakening arises.
intent_summary: The verse asks the practitioner to perceive body and world as nothing but consciousness, which leads to profound awakening.
beginner_explanation: Instead of seeing your body as ordinary matter, try feeling it as made of awareness itself. You can also expand that feeling to the whole world. When you hold this vision steadily, a sense of deep awakening can arise.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā employs bhāvanā to re-envision deha or jagat as cinmaya, thereby collapsing the usual distinction between inert object and conscious subject. The phrase yugapat suggests simultaneous holding without fragmentation into separate concepts, allowing paramodaya—highest arising—to manifest. It aligns with non-dual Śaiva doctrine that all forms are condensations of cit.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rising Through the Breath Junction
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
िायुद्वयस्य सम्घट्टाद् अन्तर् वा िवहरन्तत् ।
योगी समत्वविज्ञानसमुद्गमनभाजनम् ॥ ६४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
īyudvayasya sam्घṭṭād antar vā viharantat |
yogī समत्वविज्ञानसमुद्गमनभाजनम् || 64 ||
translation: From the collision of the two winds, or from their movement within, the yogī becomes a vessel for the arising of equalized awareness.
intent_summary: The verse points to using the meeting or movement of the two breaths to enter balanced, expansive awareness.
beginner_explanation: Feel the point where the breath changes direction, or notice the subtle movement of breath inside the body. At that exact moment, remain alert and balanced. This can open a calm, even awareness that feels wider than ordinary thinking.
scholar_explanation: Although the text is OCR-corrupted, the verse clearly describes the junction or saṅghaṭṭa of the two vāyus, a recognized VBT practice centered on breath transitions. The result is sama-tva-vijñāna, balanced cognition, in which the yogī becomes an āśraya for elevated awareness. The method parallels other kumbhaka-based dhāraṇās where prāṇa’s motion is used to reveal the steady center.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The World as One's Own Bliss
sanskrit:
सिं जगत्स्वदेहं वा स्वानन्दभवरतं स्मरेत् ।
युगपत्स्वामृतेनैि परानन्दमयो भवेत् ॥ ६५ ॥
transliteration:
sīṃ jagatsvadehaṃ vā svānandabhavaratṃ স্মaret |
yugapatsvāmṛtenaiva parānandamayo bhavet || 65 ||
translation: One should remember the world as one's own body, or as abiding in one's own bliss. By one's own nectar at once, one becomes filled with supreme bliss.
intent_summary: The verse teaches transforming perception into a felt sense of all-pervading personal bliss and unity.
