beginner_explanation: Try to feel the world as not separate from you, but as part of your own living body. Let the feeling be warm, alive, and blissful. When that sense deepens, ordinary pleasure can open into a much larger joy.
scholar_explanation: Here the practitioner is asked to स्मरेत् the jagat either as svadeha or as immersed in svānanda-bhavarata, shifting cognition into an affective non-dual register. The phrase svāmṛta points to an inner nectar or autonomously arising bliss that, when tasted simultaneously, yields parānandamaya—a fullness beyond ordinary sensory pleasure. This is a bhāvanā of identity between self, world, and blissful consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sudden Great Bliss
sanskrit:
कुहनेन प्रयोगेण सद्य एव मृगेक्षणे ।
समुदेवत महानन्दो येन तत्त्वम् प्रकाशते ॥ ६६ ॥
transliteration:
kuhanena prayogeṇa sadya eva mṛgekṣaṇe |
samud eva ta mahānando yena tattvam prakāśate || 66 ||
translation: O lady with deer-like eyes, through a skillful subtle device, immediately there arises a great bliss by which the truth becomes manifest.
intent_summary: The verse teaches a quick contemplative trick or subtle method that immediately awakens intense bliss and reveals truth.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes there is a small, clever shift in attention that changes everything at once. This verse says that by using that subtle approach, great joy can arise immediately. That joy then helps reveal what is real.
scholar_explanation: The OCR is imperfect, but the verse indicates a kuhana or ingenious upāya producing immediate mahānanda. Such methods in VBT often rely on a precise experiential pivot rather than gradual effort, and the resulting bliss is a revealer of tattva rather than merely an emotion. The address to mṛgekṣaṇī is traditional Tantric rhetoric to invite intimacy and attention.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Ascending the Inner Current
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सिधस्रोतोवनिन्धेन प्राणशक्त्योर्ध्वधया शनैः ।
वपपीलस्पशधिेलायां प्रथते परमं सुखम् ॥ ६७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
siddhasrotovandhena prāṇaśaktyordhvadhayā śanaiḥ |
viśeṣa-sparśa-līlāyāṃ prathate paramaṃ sukham || 67 ||
translation: By the closure of the perfected channel, and by the gradual upward flow of the power of prāṇa, through the play of a special touch, supreme happiness unfolds.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to guide subtle life-energy upward so that a refined touch of awareness opens into great joy.
beginner_explanation: Imagine energy rising gently through the body like a stream being guided upward. As you become sensitive to subtle contact or tingling, a very peaceful happiness can appear. The practice is soft, gradual, and inward.
scholar_explanation: Despite OCR issues, the verse points to siddha-srotas and the upward movement of prāṇa-śakti, likely a subtle yogic ascent practice. The phrase viśeṣa-sparśa suggests an exquisitely fine bodily or energetic sensation, whose recognition catalyzes parama-sukha. This integrates breath, energy, and tactile awareness in a manner consistent with VBT’s embodied soteriology.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Joy in the Interval
sanskrit:
िह्नेविधषस्य मध्ये तु वचत्तं सुखमयं वक्षपेत् ।
केिलं िायुपूणं वा स्मरानन्देन युज्यते ॥ ६८ ॥
transliteration:
hṛdaye dvividhasya madhye tu cittaṃ sukhamayaṃ kṣipet |
kevalaṃ vāyupūrṇaṃ vā smarānandena yujyate || 68 ||
translation: In the middle of the twofold heart, one should cast the mind into bliss. Or, being filled only with breath, one becomes joined with blissful remembrance.
intent_summary: The verse teaches placing the mind in the heart-center or in breath-filled fullness so that blissful awareness arises.
beginner_explanation: Bring attention to the center of the chest and let the mind sink there softly. Or simply feel the body full of breath and let that fullness become your focus. Either way, the result is a quiet joy mixed with clear presence.
scholar_explanation: The verse locates practice in hṛdaya-madhya, the heart-center that functions as a non-dual locus of consciousness in Śaiva and Tantric physiology. By casting citta into sukhamaya or dwelling in vāyu-pūrṇa fullness, the practitioner enters smarānanda, a remembrance suffused with bliss. This combines spatial interiority, breath awareness, and affective absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss Born of Union
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
शविसंगमसंक्षुब्धशक्त्यािेशािसावनकम् ।
यत्सुखम् ब्रह्मतत्त्वस्य तत्सुखम् स्वाक्यमुच्यते ॥ ६९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम |
śaktisaṅgama-saṃkṣubdha-śaktyāveśād-asāvanakam |
yat sukhaṃ brahmatattvasya tat sukhaṃ svākyam ucyate || 69 ||
translation: That bliss of Brahma-tattva is called one's own, which arises from the union of Śakti, when the power within is agitated and entered by that power.
intent_summary: The verse teaches recognizing the bliss arising from inner union with Śakti as one's own deepest nature.
beginner_explanation: When inner energy stirs and you feel a deep meeting or union within, notice the happiness that arises. The verse says this is not just ordinary pleasure; it points to your truest nature. Rest in that feeling without grabbing it.
scholar_explanation: This verse identifies sukha generated by śaktisaṅgama and śaktyāveśa as brahmatattva-sukha, explicitly equated with one’s own essential bliss (svākya). The language frames ecstatic arousal not as distraction but as a sign of the self-recognition of consciousness in dynamic form. It is a hallmark Śākta-Śaiva claim: the power that stirs is the same power that reveals the absolute.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss from Sexual Remembrance
sanskrit:
लेहनामन्थनाकोटै् स्त्रीसुखस्य भरात्स्मृते् ।
शक्त्यभावेऽवप देिेवश भिेदानन्दसम्प्लि् ॥ ७० ॥
transliteration:
lehanāmanthanakoṭaiḥ strīsukhasya bharāt smṛteḥ |
śaktyabhāve 'pi deveśi bhaved ānandasamplavaḥ || 70 ||
translation: O Lord of the gods, by remembrance of the fullness of a woman's pleasure through licking, stirring, and embracing, even in the absence of a partner, there arises a flood of bliss.
intent_summary: The verse teaches using memory and embodied recollection of sensual pleasure to evoke inner bliss without external dependence.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that even remembering intense pleasure can awaken a powerful wave of joy inside. You do not need the outer experience itself for the feeling to arise. The key is to sense it vividly and let the body-mind resonate with it.
scholar_explanation: The verse uses erotic memory (smṛti) as an upāya: the practitioner recollects strī-sukha through sensuous acts, and even without external śakti, ānanda-samplava arises. This is not merely indulgence but a Tantric interiorization of eros into contemplative bliss. The invocation to deveśi reflects the text’s ritualized, intimate dialogue form.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Joy Absorption in Bliss
sanskrit:
आनन्दे महवत प्राप्ते दृष्टे वा िान्धिे वचरात् ।
आनन्दमुद्गतम् ध्यात्वा तल्लयस्तन्मना भवेत् ॥ ७१ ॥
transliteration:
ānande mahati prāpte dṛṣṭe vā bandhīe vicārāt |
ānandam udgataṃ dhyātvā tallayaḥ tanmanā bhavet || 71 ||
translation: When great bliss has arisen, whether seen directly or through reflection, one should meditate on the bliss that has emerged; through absorption in that, the mind becomes identified with it.
intent_summary: Use an arising experience of bliss as the object of meditation so the mind dissolves into that bliss.
beginner_explanation: If a wave of joy appears, do not just notice it and move on. Rest your attention on the joy itself, as if you are gently leaning into a warm light. By staying with it, the mind begins to merge with the feeling.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses ānanda as the upāya: when mahānanda or a lesser bliss appears, the practitioner contemplates the uplifted joy (ānandam udagatam) until laya occurs and tanmanā—mind made of that—arises. It reflects the VBT method of taking a spontaneous state and intensifying nondual identification rather than resisting or analyzing it.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss from Drinking and Eating
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
जववधपानकृतोल्लासरसानन्दविजृम्भणात् ।
भाियेद्भवरतािस्थां महानन्दस्ततो भवेत् ॥ ७२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava tantraṃ |
javavadhyāna-pānakṛtollāsa-rasa-ānanda-vijṛmbhaṇāt |
bhāvayet bhava-ratāvasthāṃ mahānandas tato bhavet || 72 ||
translation: By the surge of joy and bliss born of delight produced through drinking and eating, one should contemplate the state of being absorbed in existence; then great bliss arises.
intent_summary: Transform ordinary sensory delight into a contemplative doorway to profound bliss and expanded being.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that even simple pleasures like eating or drinking can become practice. Instead of rushing through the pleasant feeling, notice how alive and open you become. If you stay with that fullness, it can deepen into a larger spiritual joy.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to rasa-ānanda arising from pāna and other sensory delights, then instructs bhāvanā on bhava-ratāvasthā, a condition of being steeped in existence itself. The ordinary aesthetic or bodily pleasure becomes a support for mahānanda, showing the Tantric revaluation of embodied life as a portal to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Identity with Tasted Experience
sanskrit:
वगतावदविषयास्वादासमसौख्यैकतात्मन् ।
योवगनस्तन्मयत्वेन मनोरूढेस् तदात्मता ॥ ७३ ॥
transliteration:
gatādi-viṣayāsvāda-samasaukhyaikatātman |
yoginaḥ tanmayatvena manoruḍheḥ tadātmatā || 73 ||
translation: For the yogin whose self is unified in the equal happiness of tasting the objects of the senses, when the mind ascends into that state through identification, there is oneness with that reality.
intent_summary: Let evenly pervading pleasure dissolve the sense of separateness until you become one with the experienced state.
beginner_explanation: Here the practice is to let a balanced feeling of pleasure fill you so evenly that there is no sense of you here and the experience over there. It is like being completely immersed in warm water and forgetting the edge of your body. That immersion is the point.
scholar_explanation: The compound samasaukhyaikatātman suggests an integrated self in homogeneous pleasure, and tanmayatva marks identity-by-penetration. The verse indicates a nondual shift in which manoruḍha, the mind having risen into that state, culminates in tadātmatā—identity with the realized condition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Holding the Mind's Satisfaction
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यि यि मनस्तुवष्टमधनस्तिैि धारयेत् ।
ति ति परानन्दस्वारूपं सम्प्रितधते ॥ ७४ ॥
transliteration:
yad yad manas-tuṣṭim adhastad vai dhārayet |
tad tad parānanda-svarūpaṃ saṃpratidhate || 74 ||
translation: Whatever gives satisfaction to the mind, one should hold to that; in each such instance, the nature of supreme bliss is manifested.
intent_summary: Use whatever truly satisfies and steadies the mind as a doorway into supreme bliss.
beginner_explanation: Notice what naturally makes your mind settle and feel content. Instead of chasing many things, stay with that settling. The calm happiness you feel can open into a deeper joy beyond the ordinary mind.
scholar_explanation: This verse universalizes the method: any source of manas-tuṣṭi can be retained as dhāraṇā, revealing parānanda-svarūpa. It emphasizes the Tantric principle that the path is not restricted to sacred or rare objects; any stable satisfaction can become a support for recognition of ultimate bliss.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Self in the Approach of Sleep
sanskrit:
अनागतायां वनद्रायां प्रणष्टे िाह्यगोचरे ।
सािस्था मनसा गम्या परा देवी प्रकाशते ॥ ७५ ॥
transliteration:
anāgatāyāṃ nidrāyāṃ praṇaṣṭe bāhyagocare |
sāvasthā manasā gamyā parā devī prakāśate || 75 ||
translation: In the sleep that has not yet arrived, when the outer field has disappeared, that state is attainable by the mind; there the Supreme Goddess shines forth.
intent_summary: Attend to the threshold before sleep and recognize the luminous awareness present as the outer world fades.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the moment just before sleep, when the world is slipping away but you are still aware. If you notice that quiet threshold instead of blacking out, something very clear and peaceful can appear. The teaching is to recognize that quiet awareness as sacred.
scholar_explanation: Anāgatā nidrā refers to the pre-sleep interval, a liminal state where bāhyagocara has vanished yet awareness persists. The verse identifies that accessible state as parā devī, aligning with VBT’s use of sandhi and transitional gaps to reveal prakāśa, the self-luminous nature of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Light in Open Space
sanskrit:
तेजसा सूयधदीपादेराकाशे शिलीकृते ।
दृवष्टवनधिेश्या तिैि स्वात्मरूपं प्रकाशते ॥ ७६ ॥
transliteration:
tejasā sūryadīpādere ākāśe śaśīlikṛte |
dṛṣṭi-niveśyā tathaiva svātma-rūpaṃ prakāśate || 76 ||
translation: When, by the brilliance of the sun, lamp, or similar light, the sky is made moonlike, if the gaze is fixed there, one’s own Self-form shines forth.
intent_summary: Use a steady gaze on a bright spacious field of light to discover the radiance of the Self.
beginner_explanation: Look at a bright, open field of light, such as sunlight or a lamp reflected in space, until it feels soft and vast rather than sharp. Then keep your attention there. The verse says that this can reveal your own inner nature as light and openness.
scholar_explanation: The practice combines tejas and ākāśa, producing a śaśīlikṛta sky-like field, and instructs dṛṣṭi-niveśa. This is a visual support leading to svātma-rūpa-prakāśa, consistent with Śaiva recognition that outward luminosity mirrors the light of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gaze with Fierce Goddess
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
करवङ्कण्या क्रोधनया भैरव्या लेलिहानया ।
खेचयाध दृवष्टकाले च परािावप्त् प्रकाशते ॥ ७७ ॥
transliteration:
karṅkanyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelīhanayā |
khecaryā dṛṣṭi-kāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate || 77 ||
translation: By the fierce, wrathful Bhairavī who licks forth, and by khecarī, during the time of gaze, supreme attainment shines forth.
intent_summary: Maintain a subtle upward or inner gaze while invoking intense, fierce awareness to awaken supreme realization.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses a strong, vivid image of the fierce Goddess and a special way of gazing. The point is to let your attention become sharp, alive, and uplifted rather than dull. In that heightened state, a deeper fulfillment can appear.
scholar_explanation: The verse combines Bhairavī imagery with khecarī-dṛṣṭi, indicating an elevated, inward or upward gaze. Parāvāpti, supreme attainment, emerges not from force alone but from the intensity and continuity of awareness aligned with Śākta-Bhairava power.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting Without Support
sanskrit:
मृद्वासने विजैकेन हस्तपादौ वनराश्रयम् ।
वनधाय तत्प्रसङ्गेन परा पूणाध मवतभधिेत् ॥ ७८ ॥
transliteration:
mṛdvāsane vijāikeṇa hastapādau nirāśrayam |
nidhāya tat-prasaṅgena parā pūrṇā matir bhavet || 78 ||
translation: Sitting on a soft seat, placing the hands and feet without support, through that contact one becomes endowed with the supreme, पूर्ण, complete understanding.
intent_summary: Let the body rest in an unsupported, relaxed posture so awareness naturally opens into completeness.
beginner_explanation: Sit comfortably and let your hands and feet be relaxed, not braced or tense. When the body feels fully supported and at ease, the mind can stop gripping. In that ease, a sense of wholeness can arise by itself.
scholar_explanation: A soft seat and nirāśrayam placement of limbs create bodily ease that supports parā pūrṇā mati, the complete or plenary mind. The verse exemplifies somatic dhāraṇā: bodily non-striving becomes the condition for the recognition of fullness, a recurring theme in Trika embodiment practice.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seated Stillness and Raised Arms
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
उपविश्यासने सम्यविाहू कृत्वाधधकुवञ्चतौ ।
कक्षव्योवि मन् कुिधन् शममायावत तल्लयात् ॥ ७९ ॥
transliteration:
upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvordhvakubcitau |
kakṣavyomni manḥ kṛtvā śamam āyāti tal-layāt || 79 ||
translation: Seated properly on the seat, with both arms raised and curved upward, by placing the mind in the space of the armpits, it comes to peace through dissolution.
intent_summary: Use a specific seated posture and bodily attention point to let the mind settle into stillness and dissolve.
beginner_explanation: This is a posture-based meditation: sit in a stable way and bring attention to the open space around the underarms. The body becomes the anchor, and the mind has less reason to wander. As attention stays there, restfulness deepens.
scholar_explanation: The instruction to place manas in the kakṣa-vyoman identifies a subtle bodily-spatial support, leading to śama through laya. Such practices show the VBT’s use of micro-embodiments where attention to a minor bodily space produces mental quieting and absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steady Gaze into Formless Support
sanskrit:
स्थूलरूपस्य भािस्य स्तब्धां दृवष्टं वनपात्य च ।
अवचरेण वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा वशिं व्रजेत् ॥ ८० ॥
transliteration:
sthūlarūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātayitvā ca |
acareṇa nirādhāraṃ manas kṛtvā śivaṃ vrajet || 80 ||
translation: Having fixed the unmoving gaze on a gross form, and making the mind unsupported by movement, one goes to Śiva.
intent_summary: Hold the gaze steady on an external form until the mind becomes supportless and enters pure Śiva-awareness.
beginner_explanation: Pick one visible object and look at it without letting your attention bounce around. At the same time, keep the mind from running off into stories. When both gaze and mind become still, a deeper silence can open.
scholar_explanation: Stabdhā dṛṣṭi on sthūlarūpa, combined with nirādhāra manas, produces entry into śiva, the nondual reality beyond objectification. The verse coordinates visual fixation with mental immobility, a classic Trika move from gross form to formless awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inner Utterance into Silence
sanskrit:
मध्यवजह्वे िावरतास्ये मध्ये वनक्षप्य चेतनाम् ।
होच्चारं मनसा कुिंस्तत् शान्ते प्रलीयते ॥ ८१ ॥
transliteration:
madhyavartī jihvāyāṃ hṛdayāsyāyāṃ madhye nikṣipya cetanām |
hocchāraṃ manasā kurvīt tat śānte pralīyate || 81 ||
translation: Placing awareness in the middle of the tongue and palate, one should mentally perform the upward utterance (hocchāra); when that becomes still, it dissolves.
intent_summary: Use a subtle inner articulation to guide awareness into stillness, where the activity of sound collapses into silence.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to focus attention on a specific inner point in the mouth while quietly making a mental upward sound. The point is not the sound itself, but the way it gathers the mind. When the inner motion settles, awareness naturally sinks into quiet.
scholar_explanation: The verse describes an internal nāda/mantra practice centered on the madhya of the tongue/palate region, with cetanā placed there and an inner hocchāra made by manas. As the subtle phonation becomes śānta, it dissolves (pralīyate), indicating a transition from sound-supported concentration into laya. This aligns with VBT techniques that use internalized phonetic energy as a bridge into nondual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting in the Unsupported Self
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
आसने शयने वस्थत्वा वनराधारं विभावयन् ।
स्वदेहं मनवस वक्षणे क्षणात्क्षीणाशयो भवेत् ॥ ८२ ॥
transliteration:
āsane śayane sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan |
sva-dehaṃ manasi kṣaṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet || 82 ||
translation: Sitting or lying down, contemplating the unsupported (nirādhāra), and placing one's own body in the mind for a moment, one becomes rid of mental tendencies in an instant.
intent_summary: Contemplate awareness without support, using the body as a temporary focus until the mind's habitual tendencies fade.
beginner_explanation: Here you simply sit or lie down and notice the feeling of being present without leaning on anything. If you briefly hold your body in mind, as if observing it from the inside, the mind begins to loosen. With practice, old patterns can drop away very quickly.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā emphasizes nirādhāra-vibhāvanā, contemplation of the supportless ground of consciousness, regardless of posture (āsana or śayana). By holding sva-deha in manas only momentarily, the practitioner sees body as an object within awareness, leading to kṣīṇāśaya, the attenuation of latent dispositions. The technique is explicitly nondual: awareness is not produced but recognized as unsupported and self-existing.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Stillness through Gentle Movement
sanskrit:
चलासने वस्थतस्याथ शनैिाध देहचालनात् ।
प्रशान्ते मानसे भावे देवि वदव्यौघम् आप्नुयात् ॥ ८३ ॥
transliteration:
calāsane sthitasyaatha śanair vā deha-cālanāt |
śānte mānase bhāve devi divyaugham āpnuyāt || 83 ||
translation: While seated in a moving posture, or by gently moving the body, when the mental state becomes peaceful, O Devi, one attains the stream of the divine.
intent_summary: Use mild bodily motion as a way to calm the mind until a deeper divine current appears.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that even gentle movement can be a doorway to meditation. If you sit or move slowly and keep the mind soft and शांत/peaceful, a subtler inner experience may arise. The body is used like a rocking boat that helps the mind settle into calm water.
scholar_explanation: The text allows cālāsana, a posture with movement, or deliberate deha-cālana to induce śānta mānasa-bhāva. Once mental turbulence subsides, divyaugha, the 'stream of the divine,' arises spontaneously, indicating grace-like influx into refined consciousness. The method shows that stillness need not be forced; regulated motion can reveal the underlying steadiness of caitanya.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorption in Clear Sky
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
आकाशं विमलं पश्यन्कृत्वा दृवष्टं वनरन्तराम् ।
स्तब्धात्मा तत्क्षणाद्देवि भैरवं िपुराप्नुयात् ॥ ८४ ॥
transliteration:
ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantarām |
stabdhātmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || 84 ||
translation: Seeing the pure, clear sky and keeping one's gaze continuous and unmoving, with the self made still, one immediately attains the body of Bhairava, O Devi.
intent_summary: Fix the gaze on clear open space until the mind becomes motionless and identifies with Bhairava's expansive nature.
beginner_explanation: Look at open sky or a clear expanse without letting your attention jump around. As your gaze stays steady, your inner feeling of being a separate, busy self can pause. In that quiet openness, you may sense a vast presence rather than a small individual self.
scholar_explanation: This practice uses bahiṣ-ākāśa as a visual support for internal expansion: vimalam ākāśam and nirantarā dṛṣṭi dissolve reactive cognition. When the self becomes stabdha, the practitioner 'attains Bhairava-vapu,' meaning recognition of one's own consciousness as identical with the expansive Bhairava state. The verse connects visual openness with chidakāśa-like recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Light at the Crown
sanskrit:
लीनं मूवनध वियत्सिधम् भैरवत्वेन भाियेत् ।
तत्सिधम् भैरवाकारतेजस्तत्त्वं समाविशेत् ॥ ८५ ॥
transliteration:
līnaṃ mūrdhni viyat-sphuṭam bhairavatvena bhāvayet |
tat-sphuṭaṃ bhairavākāratējastattvaṃ samāviśet || 85 ||
translation: One should contemplate the clearly manifest expanse, absorbed in the crown of the head, as Bhairavahood; then one enters that manifest luminous essence having the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Visualize the subtle space at the crown as Bhairava's radiant nature and merge into that light-essence.
beginner_explanation: Bring attention to the top of the head and imagine a bright, open space there. Instead of thinking of it as just your body, feel it as living presence or light. If you stay with that feeling, the sense of self can merge into a wider, radiant awareness.
scholar_explanation: The crown center (mūrdhan) becomes the locus for viyat-sphuṭa, the 'clearly manifested space,' to be contemplated as bhairavatva. The practitioner then enters tattva in the form of bhairavākāra-tejas, a luminous principle expressing Bhairava as radiance rather than object. This is a classic śiro-grahaṇa/ūrdhva-ākāśa visualization leading to identity with consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वकवञ्चज्ज्ञातम् द्वैतदावय बाह्यालोकस्तम् पुन् ।
विश्वावद भैरवं रूपं ज्ञात्वानन्तप्रकाशभृत् ॥ ८६ ॥
transliteration:
kiñcid jñātaṃ dvaita-dāvi bhiḥ bāhyāloka-stam punar |
viśvādibhir bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ jñātvānantaprakāśa-bhṛt || 86 ||
translation: Having known even a little, and by burning up duality, and the outer light again subdued, one should know the form of Bhairava as beginning with the whole universe; then one is filled with infinite प्रकाश (light/awareness).
intent_summary: Overcome dualistic perception and recognize the entire visible world as Bhairava's form, shining as infinite awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a shift in how you see the world. Instead of viewing things as separate objects, let that separation burn away until everything appears as one living presence. Then the world itself becomes a doorway into vast, bright awareness.
scholar_explanation: The text presents a nondual re-seeing in which kiñcid jñāta, even partial insight, is enough to ignite the dvaita-dāvi—'burning up' duality—while bāhyāloka is stilled. When viśva and the rest are recognized as bhairava-rūpa, the practitioner abides as anantaprakāśa-bhṛt, bearer of limitless luminosity. The verse is doctrinally central: world appearance is not rejected but transfigured as the deity's own form.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Moonlit Night Contemplation
sanskrit:
एवमेि दुवनधशायां कृष्णपक्षागमे वचरम् ।
तैवमरं भावयन् रूपं भैरवं रूपमेष्यवत ॥ ८७ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva duṃdihśāyāṃ kṛṣṇapakṣāgame ciram |
taimiraṃ bhāvayan rūpaṃ bhairavaṃ rūpam eṣyati || 87 ||
translation: In the same way, during a dark night at the arrival of the dark fortnight, for a long time contemplating the dark form, one attains the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: Use the darkness of night as a meditative image to enter Bhairava's formless, subtle presence.
beginner_explanation: The verse recommends meditating at night, especially when it is dark and quiet. Instead of resisting the darkness, you let it become the object of contemplation. Over time, the darkness stops feeling empty and becomes a way to sense a deeper presence.
scholar_explanation: Here the temporal condition of kṛṣṇapakṣāgama and duṃdihśā (darkness/night) functions as a tantric support for taimiram bhāvayan, contemplating the dark aspect as Bhairava-rūpa. The practice leverages external darkness to induce inward subtlety, where absence of visible form points to the formless presence of consciousness. It complements solar or luminous visualizations by showing that obscurity too can disclose the divine.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Eyes Half-Closed in Darkness
sanskrit:
एवमेि वनमील्यादौ नेिे कृष्णाभमाग्रत् ।
प्रसायध भैरवं रूपं भाियम्स्तन्मयो भवेत् ॥ ८८ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva nimīlyādau netre kṛṣṇābham agrataḥ |
prasārya bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ bhāvayan tan-mayo bhavet || 88 ||
translation: Likewise, at the beginning with the eyes half-closed, and with darkness-like blackness before one, extending the gaze and contemplating the form of Bhairava, one becomes identified with that.
intent_summary: Let the half-closed gaze and dim visual field become a doorway into Bhairava-identification.
beginner_explanation: You relax your eyes until they are partly closed and look into the dark, soft field in front of you. Instead of straining, you simply rest in that dimness and imagine it as Bhairava's presence. Staying there gently can make you feel merged with it.
scholar_explanation: The verse prescribes nimīlya, half-closing the eyes, with kṛṣṇābha, a blackish or dark visual field, as a support for bhairava-rūpa-bhāvanā. By prasārya, extending the gaze without fixation, one enters tanmaya, identity with the contemplated form. This is a subtle liminal visual dhāraṇā between external sight and internal absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entry through Sense Interruption
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यस्य कस्येवन्द्रयस्यावप व्याघाताच्च वनरोधत् ।
प्रविष्टस्याद्वये शून्ये तिैिात्मा प्रकाशते ॥ ८९ ॥
transliteration:
yasya kasyendriyasyaapi vyāghātāc ca nirodhataḥ |
praviṣṭasyādvaye śūnye tatrāivātmā prakāśate || 89 ||
translation: When any sense faculty is interrupted and restrained, upon entering the nondual void, there the Self shines forth.
intent_summary: Use sensory interruption as a doorway into the nondual void where the Self becomes self-evident.
beginner_explanation: If one of your senses is briefly blocked or interrupted, attention can turn inward. The verse says that when this happens and you enter a deep inner emptiness, your true self shows up clearly. It is like noticing the room's silence after a loud sound stops.
scholar_explanation: Any indriya-āghāta or nirodha can function as an entry point into advaya-śūnya, the nondual void where subject-object structuring ceases. In that gap, ātmā prakāśate—self-luminosity becomes evident without mediation. This is an important VBT principle: interruption, not addition, can reveal consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: A-U-M Into Sudden Illumination
sanskrit:
अविन्दुम् अविसगधम् च अकारम् जपतो महान् ।
उदेवत देवि सहसा ज्ञानौघ् परमेश्वर् ॥ ९० ॥
transliteration:
a-binduṃ a-visargaṃ ca akāraṃ japato mahān |
udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ || 90 ||
translation: For one who recites the great A, the bindu, the visarga, and the letter A, O Devi, suddenly arises a flood of knowledge, the supreme Lord.
intent_summary: Repeat sacred sound-elements until they spontaneously open into a surge of awakened knowledge.
beginner_explanation: This verse uses seed-sounds and subtle sound-parts as a meditation object. By repeating them carefully, the mind can suddenly brighten, as if a lamp were switched on inside. The practice is less about pronunciation than about letting sound awaken awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse centers on ā-kāra with bindu and visarga, likely referring to phonemic constituents of praṇava or related mantra-consciousness. Continuous japa culminates in sahasā, a sudden emergence of jñānaugha, because sound-form here functions as a direct carrier of śakti. The result is parameśvara, not as external deity but as the awakened plenitude of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attunement to the End of the Sound
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वर्णस्य सविसर्गस्य विसर्गान्तं चेतनं कुरु ।
निराधारेण चित्तेन स्पृशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ९१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम्
varṇasya savisargasya visargāntaṃ cetanaṃ kuru |
nirādhāreṇa cittena spṛśed brahma sanātanam || 91 ||
translation: Make consciousness rest on the end of a syllable together with its visarga; with a supportless mind, one should touch the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Use the fading edge of a sound as a doorway into supportless awareness of the eternal.
beginner_explanation: Listen closely not only to a sound itself, but to the moment it disappears. At that tiny edge, let your mind become still and simply stay there. The teaching is that even a vanishing sound can open into a deeper silence.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā directs awareness to the visarga-anta of varṇa, the terminal release of a phoneme, and then asks for nirādhāra-citta, mind without any prop. The practice uses the phonemic dissolution point as a liminal opening into Brahman, akin to other VBT sound-based techniques where nāda becomes a support for transcending sound itself. It relies on the Tantric insight that cessation is not mere absence but a charged threshold of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the Sky-Like Self
sanskrit:
व्योमाकारं स्वमात्मानम् ध्यायेवद्दवग्भरनािृतम् ।
निराश्रया चित्त् शवि् स्वरूपं दशधयेत्तदा ॥ ९२ ॥
transliteration:
vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānam dhyāyed ākāśabharaṇāt |
nirāśrayā citte śaktiḥ svarūpaṃ darśayettadā || 92 ||
translation: One should meditate on one’s own Self as sky-like, filled with space; when the mind is without support, the power reveals its own nature.
intent_summary: Contemplate the self as limitless space so the mind can become empty and reveal its true power.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your true self is like the open sky: vast, clear, and unbroken. If you stop clinging to thoughts and labels, that inner openness becomes obvious. In that openness, something deeper than ordinary thinking shines forth.
scholar_explanation: Here the ātmā is visualized as vyomākāra, having the form of space, with the mind made nirāśraya, supportless. The verse suggests that when subjective constructions fall away, śakti-svarūpa—consciousness-power in its own nature—discloses itself. This aligns with VBT’s frequent equation of inner spaciousness with non-dual recognition rather than a mere blank void.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Piercing the Body with Attention
sanskrit:
किंचिदङ्गम् विभिद्यादौ तीक्ष्णसूच्यावदना तत् ।
तथैव चेतनां युक्त्वा भैरवे निर्मला गतिः ॥ ९३ ॥
transliteration:
kiṃcid aṅgaṃ vibhidya ādyau tīkṣṇa-sūcyāvadānataḥ |
tathaiva cetanāṃ yuktvā bhairave nirmalā gatiḥ || 93 ||
translation: After first piercing some part of the body as if with a sharp needle, and in the same way joining consciousness [to that point], there is a pure movement into Bhairava.
intent_summary: Fix attention sharply on a tiny bodily point so consciousness can enter a clear, Bhairava-like state.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to focus on a very small point in the body, almost as if touching it with a needle. The intensity of that narrow focus can steady the mind. From there, awareness becomes very clear and concentrated.
scholar_explanation: The instruction uses deha-pradeśa as a precise tactile locus, likened to tīkṣṇa-sūcī, to concentrate cetanā. Such micro-localized attention creates an entry into nirmalā gati, a purified movement or flow of consciousness into Bhairava. The technique belongs to the body-centered dhāraṇās that transform sensory intensity into non-dual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Freedom from Thought-Construction
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वचत्ताद्यन्त्कृवतनाधवस्त ममान्तभाधियेवदवत ।
विकल्पानामभावेन विकल्पैरुवितो भवेत् ॥ ९४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम्
cittādi-anta-kṛta-nātha-vastu mama anta-bhāvayedit |
vikalpānām abhāvena vikalpair udito bhavet || 94 ||
translation: One should contemplate that the Lord and the reality of my own being are made at both the beginning and end of thought; by the absence of conceptual constructions (vikalpas), one becomes risen through concepts.
intent_summary: See that the self and the divine stand before and after thought, then let concepts fall away into non-conceptual awareness.
beginner_explanation: Thoughts come and go, but this verse points to what is present before a thought begins and after it ends. If you stop chasing the story in your head, you can notice a quieter awareness underneath it. Paradoxically, letting go of thought can reveal a deeper clarity beyond thought.
scholar_explanation: The verse is textually difficult, but its practical thrust is clear: investigate the anta and ādi of citta, where conceptuality (vikalpa) arises and subsides, and recognize the underlying vastu/nātha as present there. By abhāva of vikalpa, one is udito—arisen or illumined—through vikalpa, i.e., concepts are seen as transparent rather than binding. This is a classic VBT move from discursive mind to non-discursive recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Through Māyā's Divisions
sanskrit:
माया विमोवहनी नाम कलाया् कलनं वस्थतम् ।
इत्यावदधमं तत्त्वानां कलयन्न पृथग्भवेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
transliteration:
māyā vimohinī nāma kalāyāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam |
ityādyaṃ tattvānāṃ kalayan na pṛthag bhavet || 95 ||
translation: Māyā, the deluder, is said to consist in the delimitation of kala; thus, while discerning the principles beginning with kala, one does not become separate.
intent_summary: Recognize that apparent divisions are māyā's construction and do not take them as truly separate.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the feeling of being cut off into separate pieces is part of illusion. If you can see the mind making those divisions, they lose some of their power. Then you remain more whole and less fragmented.
scholar_explanation: Māyā is identified as vimohinī, the deluding power that operates through kalā, delimitation or part-making. By observing the tattvas beginning with kalā without reifying them, one remains non-separate, indicating a recognition of their functional but not absolute status. The verse therefore supports a non-dual reading of cosmological categories as disclosures of consciousness rather than independently real entities.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Calming the Emerging Desire
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
झवगतीच्छां समुत्पन्नामिलोक्य शमं नयेत् ।
यत एव समुद्भूता ततस्तिैि लीयते ॥ ९६ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम्
jhaṭigatīcchāṃ samutpannām ilokya śamaṃ nayet |
yata eva samudbhūtā tatas tadvai līyate || 96 ||
translation: Seeing a desire that has suddenly arisen, one should bring it to rest; for from whatever it has arisen, in that very source it dissolves.
intent_summary: Notice a desire as it arises and let it settle back into the source from which it emerged.
beginner_explanation: When a strong want or impulse suddenly appears, don’t fight it or follow it. Just notice it clearly and let it quiet down by itself. The idea is that every desire fades back into the deeper place it came from.
scholar_explanation: The technique uses the moment of jhaṭi-udaya, abrupt emergence of icchā, as an opportunity for śama rather than expression or suppression. Since the desire arises from a source that is itself consciousness, it can be reabsorbed into that source, demonstrating the laya of affective movement. This verse is closely related to other methods of working with bhāva, impulse, and emotional surges as gateways rather than obstacles.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding Where Desire and Knowledge Do Not Arise
sanskrit:
यदा ममेच्छा नोत्पन्ना ज्ञानं वा कस्तदावस्म िै ।
तत्त्वतोऽहम् तथाभूतस्तल्लीनस्तन्मना भवेत् ॥ ९७ ॥
transliteration:
yadā mamecchā notpannā jñānaṃ vā kas tadā vasmi |
tattvato 'ham tathābhūtas tallīnas tanmanā bhavet || 97 ||
translation: When my desire has not arisen, nor knowledge—what am I then? In truth I am just that; becoming absorbed in it, one should be minded toward that.
intent_summary: Rest in the state before desire and conceptual knowing, and identify with that bare reality.
beginner_explanation: Ask yourself what you are when there is no urge and no thought saying what you are. This verse points to the quiet presence that remains even then. If you stay with that presence, your mind naturally settles into it.
scholar_explanation: The verse employs radical self-inquiry: when icchā and jñāna have not yet emerged, what remains? The answer is tattvataḥ aham—this very reality, implying pure subjectivity prior to objectifying movement, and one becomes tanmaya/tanmanas by absorption. It resonates with the VBT’s repeated invitation to recognize the gap before cognitive and volitional emergence as Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steadying the Mind in Desire or Knowledge
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
इच्छायामथिा ज्ञाने जाते वचत्तं वनिेशयेत् ।
आत्मिुद्ध्यानन्यचेतास्ततस्तत्त्वाथधदशधनम् ॥ ९८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tant्रम्
ecchāyām athavā jñāne jāte cittaṃ niveśayet |
ātmaśuddhyānanyacetās tatastattvārthadarśanam || 98 ||
translation: When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should place the mind there; through purification of the Self and one-pointedness, there is then perception of the reality of the principle.
intent_summary: Use either desire or knowing itself as the focus for one-pointed awareness, until truth is directly seen.
beginner_explanation: If a strong desire or a clear thought appears, don’t automatically push it away. Instead, rest your attention in it without getting lost. With a calm and steady mind, you can see more deeply into what it really is.
scholar_explanation: This verse reverses ordinary aversion to mental events by instructing citta-niveśana in icchā or jñāna itself. Through ātma-śuddhi and ananya-cetas, one arrives at tattvārtha-darśana, direct apprehension of reality as it is. The method reflects the Tantric principle that any strong state, properly held, can function as an access point to recognition rather than bondage.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Knowledge as Supportless
sanskrit:
वनवनधवमत्तं भिेज्ज्ञानम् वनराधारं भ्रमात्मकम् ।
तत्त्वत् कस्यवचन्नैतद् एवम्भािी वशि् वप्रये ॥ ९९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānam eva bhaved jñānam nirādhāraṃ bhramātmakam |
tattvatas kasyacid etad evaṃ bhāvī śiva priye || 99 ||
translation: Knowledge itself should be known as supportless and of the nature of भ्रम; in truth, this is not of anyone—so, O beloved of Śiva, let this be contemplated thus.
intent_summary: Recognize even knowledge as unsupported and fleeting, and do not make it into a possession or fixed view.
beginner_explanation: This verse warns that even your smartest ideas are not solid ground. Thoughts and insights can come and go like dreams. If you see them that way, you won’t cling to them as “mine,” and the mind becomes freer.
scholar_explanation: Jñāna here is said to be nirādhāra and bhramātmaka, indicating that even cognition is unstable and non-absolute. By refusing to ascribe ultimate ownership or substantiality to knowledge—kasyacid etat na—it serves the devotional-recognition move of the text: all epistemic forms are understood within Śiva-consciousness. This prepares the practitioner for ungrounded awareness rather than refined conceptual certainty.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing All Bodies as Consciousness
sanskrit:
वचद्धमाध सिधदेहेषु विशेषो नावस्त कुिवचत् ।
अतश्च तन्मयं सिं भावयन्भिवजज्जन् ॥ १०० ॥
transliteration:
ciddharmā sarvadeheṣu viśeṣo nāsti kutracit |
ataś ca tanmayaṃ sarvaṃ bhāvayann bhajet janan || 100 ||
translation: The nature of consciousness is the same in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere. Therefore, contemplating all as made of That, one should worship the arising of beings.
intent_summary: See the same consciousness in every body and regard all forms of life as expressions of it.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that the deepest reality in everyone is the same. If you look at people and creatures that way, separation softens. Then everyday life becomes a kind of reverent seeing.
scholar_explanation: Ciddharma is asserted to be uniform across sarvadeha, with no viśeṣa anywhere, a strong non-dual statement of universal consciousness. The practitioner is instructed to bhāvayann sarvaṃ tanmayaṃ, perceiving all entities as permeated by that one reality, which culminates in a devotional mode of honoring manifestation itself. This verse bridges contemplative insight and ethical universality, characteristic of mature Trika recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transcending the Defiling Passions
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कामक्रोधलोभमोहमदमात्सयधगोचरे ।
िुवद्धं वनवस्तवमतां कृत्वा तत्तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
transliteration:
kāma-krodha-lobha-moha-mada-mātsarya-dhāgocare |
buddhaṃ nivastamitaṃ kṛtvā tat tattvam aviśiṣyate || 101 ||
translation: In the field of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and such stains, having made the intellect still and completely restrained, one becomes identical with that reality.
intent_summary: Use the pressure of strong emotions and mental impurities as a field for making the mind still until nondual reality shines through.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to run away from difficult emotions, but to let them settle instead of following them. When the mind stops getting pulled around by desire, anger, and jealousy, a deeper truth can be noticed. It is like muddy water becoming clear when left undisturbed.
scholar_explanation: The verse places sādhana in the midst of kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, and mātsarya, but directs one to make the buddhi ni-sthita/nivastamita. In the settled state, the practitioner does not merely suppress afflictions; rather, the tattva is recognized as untouched by the modifications. This aligns with VBT’s broader strategy of using any strong state as a doorway to bhairava-consciousness, not as an object of moral rejection.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Illusion
sanskrit:
इन्द्रजालमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं वा वचिकमधित् ।
भ्रमद्वा ध्यायत् सिं पश्यतश्च सुखोद्गम् ॥ १०२ ॥
transliteration:
indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā vicikīrṣaṇāt |
bhramad vā dhyāyan sarvaṃ paśyatas ca sukhodgamaḥ || 102 ||
translation: The world is like an illusion or a magical show, scattered or whirling; by meditating on it in this way, for one who sees everything, there arises an increase of ease and joy.
intent_summary: Contemplate the world as a shifting play of appearances so that ordinary grasping relaxes and a joyful spaciousness appears.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to look at life as if it were a magic show. Things still appear, but you stop taking them as solid and fixed. That change of view can bring a surprising sense of ease.
scholar_explanation: The viśva is described as indrajālamaya, emphasizing māyā-like display rather than ontological solidity. The practice is a cognitive reframing that loosens identification with appearances and allows the draṣṭṛ to rest in a more panoramic, non-grasping mode. This is not nihilism but a shift from reified objecthood to lila-like display within consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dwelling in the Middle of Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न वचत्तं वनवक्षपेद् दु्खे न सुखे वा पवरवक्षपेत् ।
भैरवि ज्ञायतां मध्ये वकं तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
transliteration:
na cittaṃ nikṣipet duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet |
bhairavi jñāyatāṃ madhye kiṃ tattvam aviśiṣyate || 103 ||
translation: Do not cast the mind into sorrow, nor throw it into pleasure. O Bhairavī, know the middle: what reality remains distinct there?
intent_summary: Rest in the middle ground beyond reactive pleasure and pain, and discover the reality that is not divided by opposites.
beginner_explanation: Instead of getting swept up by sadness or chasing pleasure, this verse asks you to stay centered. If you can remain steady in the middle, you may notice something in you that is bigger than both feelings. It is like standing on firm ground while waves rise and fall.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā neutralizes the duḥkha-sukha polarity and points to madhya, a classic Śaiva locus of revelation. The mind is not to be projected outward into affective extremes, but held in an unconditioned witnessing that reveals aviśiṣṭa tattva. The verse resonates strongly with VBT’s emphasis on the interval (madhya) as a doorway to Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: I Am This Bodyless Identity
sanskrit:
विहाय वनजदेहस्थं सिधिास्मीवत भावयन् ।
दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येवक्षण्या सुखी भवेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
transliteration:
vihāya nija-deha-sthaṃ siddho 'smi iti bhāvayan |
dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣaṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||
translation: Abandoning the idea of being confined to one's own body, one should contemplate, 'I am perfected.' With a firm mind and gaze, looking at nothing else, one becomes happy.
intent_summary: Replace bodily self-limitation with the sense of already being complete, and hold that conviction steadily.
beginner_explanation: Here you practice seeing yourself as more than the physical body. You quietly repeat and feel, “I am accomplished,” while keeping your attention steady. This can create a deep sense of confidence and ease.
scholar_explanation: The verse prescribes a bhāvanā of siddho ’smi, coupled with de-identification from deha-stha egoic constriction. The steady dṛṣṭi and manas prevent scattering into other objects, allowing the practitioner to inhabit the already-complete state. This is a visualized identity-shift that supports recognition of innate siddhatva, a recurring Kaśmīr Śaiva theme.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Recognizing Consciousness Everywhere
sanskrit:
घटादौ यच्च विज्ञानवमच्छाद्यं वा ममान्तरे ।
नैि सिधगतं जातं भाियवन्नवत सिधग् ॥ १०५ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare |
neva siddhaṃ na jātaṃ bhāvayan nitya-siddhagaḥ || 105 ||
translation: Whatever consciousness is in a pot and so on, or within me through desire and the like, by contemplating that it is neither accomplished nor newly arisen, one abides in eternal accomplishment.
intent_summary: See consciousness as present in all things and contemplate it as neither produced nor gained, but eternally already here.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that awareness is not something that suddenly appears or gets created. Whether you notice it in a jar, a thought, or inside yourself, it is always already there. If you reflect on that, you can feel grounded in something permanent.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of ghaṭa and ādi evokes the pervasiveness of vijñāna across containers and states, rejecting origination (jāta) and accomplishment as temporal events. By recognizing consciousness as nitya-siddha, the practitioner aligns with the non-productive, ever-present nature of cit. The verse supports a pan-consciousness vision in which inner and outer are not ultimately separate.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Watching the Subject-Object Split
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ग्राह्यग्राहकसवित्त्वं सामान्या सिद्धदेवधनानाम् ।
योगिनां तु विशेषोऽस्ति सम्बन्धे सािधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
transliteration:
grāhya-grāhaka-sattvaṃ sāmānyaṃ siddhadehinām |
yogināṃ tu viśeṣo 'sti sambandhe sāvadhānatā || 106 ||
translation: For perfected beings, the existence of the grasped and the grasper is ordinary. But for yogins, the special practice is mindfulness in relation to that connection.
intent_summary: Notice the subject-object structure itself, and remain alert to it without unconsciously falling into it.
beginner_explanation: Normally, we feel like there is a “me” looking at a separate “thing.” This verse says advanced practice is to notice that split very clearly. When you see it, you are less trapped by it.
scholar_explanation: Grāhya-grāhaka-sattva is treated as sādhāraṇa for siddha-deha awareness, yet the yogin’s distinctive discipline is sāvadhānatā regarding the sambandha itself. This suggests a subtle witnessing of relational cognition rather than mere object-absorption. The verse marks a transitional insight from dualistic perception toward the nondual recognition of consciousness as the ground of relation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Expanding into Other Bodies
sanskrit:
स्विदन्यशरीरेऽपि सवित्त्वं अनुभावयेत् ।
अपेक्षां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्यापी भवेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
transliteration:
svasmin dehāntare 'pi ca sattvaṃ anubhāvayet |
apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī bhavet || 107 ||
translation: One should experience the same reality even in another's body; abandoning attachment to one's own body, one becomes all-pervading.
intent_summary: Loosen identification with your own body and feel consciousness as equally present in others, expanding into universality.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to stop feeling that awareness belongs only to your own body. Try to sense the same life in others as in yourself. When that happens, your sense of being separate gets much wider.
scholar_explanation: The practice extends sattva/anubhava beyond the limits of sva-deha into dehāntara, dissolving possessive identification. By dropping apekṣā toward one’s own body, the yogin becomes vyāpin, echoing a hallmark Śaiva attribute of consciousness as all-pervasive. This has clear ethical and contemplative implications, since others are no longer experienced as fundamentally “other.”

speaker: Bhairava
title: Emptying the Mind of Options
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा विकल्पान्न विकल्पयेत् ।
तदात्मपरमात्मत्वे भैरवो मृगलोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
transliteration:
nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet |
tad ātma-paramātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane || 108 ||
translation: Having made the mind without support, one should not construct any further options or imaginations. O deer-eyed one, in that identity of Self and Supreme Self, there is Bhairava.
intent_summary: Withdraw the mind from all supports and conceptual constructions so that the identity of self and supreme self is directly recognized.
beginner_explanation: Here you let the mind become unsupported, like resting in open space. Instead of making plans, stories, or mental pictures, you simply stay open. In that openness, the boundary between “me” and the highest reality can fade.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāra-manas is a classic non-objective meditative state in which vikalpa is not re-generated. The revelation of ātma-paramātmatva is not an intellectual conclusion but a direct recognition of Bhairava as the identity underlying self and supreme self. The verse strongly centralizes nonconceptual awareness and is one of the clearest expressions of VBT’s nondual core.

speaker: Bhairava
title: I Am That Great Lord
sanskrit:
सिधज्ञ् सिधकताध च व्यापक् परमेश्वर् ।
स एवाहम् शैिधमाध इवत दार्ढ्ाधवच्छिो भवेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
transliteration:
siddhaṃ siddhakṛtā caiva vyāpakaṃ parameśvaram |
sa evāhaṃ śaivamārga iti dārḍhyād dhi bhavet || 109 ||
translation: The perfected and the one who makes perfection, the all-pervading Supreme Lord—he indeed is I. In the Śaiva path, one becomes firm in this conviction.
intent_summary: Stabilize the direct certainty that your own identity is the all-pervading Supreme Lord.
beginner_explanation: This verse is about becoming deeply certain that your true nature is not small or separate. It says the same presence that perfects everything is also who you really are. The practice is to let that understanding become unshakable.
scholar_explanation: Here siddha, siddhakṛtā, and parameśvara converge in an explicit ahaṃ identity statement, characteristic of Śaiva recognition (pratyabhijñā) logic. The verse does not propose a metaphorical likeness but a firm dārḍhya in the identity of the practitioner with the all-pervading Lord. It closes the sequence of recognition-style practices by turning insight into stabilized conviction.

speaker: Bhairava
title: All Waves Are Mine
sanskrit:
जलस्येिोमधयो िह्नेर्ज्ाधलाभङ्ग्य् प्रभा रिे् ।
ममैि भैरवस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेवदता् ॥ ११० ॥
transliteration:
jalasyedhodayo hy agner jvālābhaṅgyaḥ prabhā raveḥ |
mamaiva bhairavasyaitā viśvabhaṅgyo vibheditāḥ || 110 ||
translation: The waves of water, the flames of fire, and the rays of the sun—all these patterns of the world are indeed distinguished as mine, belonging to Bhairava.
intent_summary: Perceive all differentiated forms in the world as expressions of Bhairava's own power and play.
beginner_explanation: Think of the world’s many shapes like waves, flames, and sunlight—different forms, but all belonging to the same reality. This verse helps you see diversity without feeling separate from it. Everything becomes an expression of one great presence.
scholar_explanation: By comparing world-forms to waves, flames, and rays, the verse frames viśvabhaṅgyaḥ as differentiated displays of a single underlying power. The possessive “mamaiva bhairavasya” is a strong nondual claim: multiplicity is not rejected but re-read as Bhairava’s own vibheda. The practice supports perceptual re-enchantment, where distinction remains yet no longer implies ontological separation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Shock-Induced Stillness
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्ववरतम् भुवि पातनात् ।
क्षोभशविविरामेण परा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tv avarataṃ bhuvi pātanāt |
kṣobhaśavivirāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā || 111 ||
translation: By whirling again and again with the body, or by falling to the ground without pause, when the agitation comes to rest, the supreme state arises.
intent_summary: Use intense bodily motion and its sudden cessation to bring the mind into a supreme, still state.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a surprising method: move the body so intensely that the ordinary mind is shaken, then let the motion stop completely. In that gap, awareness can open into a deeper stillness. It is like spinning until your usual sense of balance breaks, then noticing the quiet after the spin ends.
scholar_explanation: The practice uses kṣobha, bodily agitation, as a doorway to kṣobha-śavi-viviraama, the cessation of disturbance. The “parā daśā” is not produced by effort alone but revealed when the oscillation of embodied activity collapses. This fits the VBT’s recurring strategy of leveraging extremes of experience to reveal the underlying consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Awakening at the End of Agitation
sanskrit:
आधारेष्वथिाऽशक्त्याऽज्ञानावच्चित्तलयेन वा ।
जातशविसमावेशक्षोभान्ते भैरवं िपु् ॥ ११२ ॥
transliteration:
ādhāreṣv athaśaktyājñānāvac cittalayena vā |
jātaśavi-samāveśa-kṣobhānte bhairavaṃ piba || 112 ||
translation: Or in the supports, or through powerlessness and unknowing, or by dissolution of mind; at the end of the disturbance of the awakened power, one should drink Bhairava.
intent_summary: Enter Bhairava by letting mental activity dissolve after the surge of awakened power or by resting in the supports with no effort.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that after a strong inner movement settles down, something deeper can be directly tasted. It can happen when the mind becomes quiet, when effort runs out, or when awareness rests on simple supports. The image of “drinking Bhairava” means absorbing that state completely.
scholar_explanation: The text points to ādhāra-practices, śakti-samāveśa, and cittalaya as alternative thresholds to the same recognition. The phrase “piba bhairavam” is an experiential injunction: assimilate the Bhairava-state rather than merely observe it. This verse emphasizes post-kṣobha openness, aligning with śāktopāya and direct absorption into nondual awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing with Unblinking Eyes
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम्प्रदायवममं देवि शृणु सम्यविदाम्यहम् ।
कैवल्यं जायते सद्यो नेत्रयोः स्तब्धमात्रयोः ॥ ११३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
saṃpradāyam imaṃ devi śṛṇu samyak vadāmy aham |
kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayor || 113 ||
translation: Devi, listen well to this tradition I now teach: liberation arises at once when the eyes become completely still.
intent_summary: Fix the eyes in unmoving stillness so that immediate liberation can arise.
beginner_explanation: Here Bhairava says that if the eyes stop moving and become perfectly steady, the mind can also become steady. This is not about staring hard, but about resting in a quiet, unblinking gaze. That calm can open into freedom right away.
scholar_explanation: Netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayor indicates a stabilizing of visual activity such that the gaze no longer fragments into subject-object grasping. Kaivalya here is immediate (sadyaḥ), suggesting that sensory stillness can expose the self-luminous ground. This verse belongs to the VBT’s sensory-entry methods, akin to trataka but aimed at dissolving vikalpa rather than concentrating on an object.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Withdrawing the Senses Inward
sanskrit:
सम्कोचं कर्णयोः कृत्वा ह्यधोद्वारे तथैव च ।
अनच्कमहलं ध्यायविशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
transliteration:
saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathāiva ca |
anacakam ahaṃ dhyāyec chuddhaṃ brahma sanātanam || 114 ||
translation: Having contracted the ears and likewise the lower opening, one should meditate on the uncaused self as the eternal, pure Brahman.
intent_summary: Withdraw sensory and bodily openings inward and contemplate the uncaused Self as eternal Brahman.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches a kind of inward closing of the senses and body. When attention turns away from outside inputs, it becomes easier to notice the quiet awareness that is always present. The goal is to recognize yourself not as the body, but as the timeless reality behind it.
scholar_explanation: The instruction to saṃkoca, contraction, of the ears and adhodvāra, the lower aperture, indicates a yogic sealing of sensory and pranic outflow. The object of meditation is anacakam aham—“the uncaused I”—identified with śuddhaṃ brahma sanātanam. The method combines bodily withdrawal with nondual contemplation, a classic VBT fusion of haṭha-like control and jñāna-recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mindlessness in the Vast Void
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
कूपावदके महागते वस्थित्वोपरि निरीक्षणात् ।
अविकल्पमते् सम्यक्सद्यवश्चत्तलय् िुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
kuppāvadake mahāgate avasthitvo parīkṣaṇāt |
avikalpamateḥ samyak sadyaś cittalayaṃ bhavet || 115 ||
translation: Standing at the mouth of a well or a great precipice and looking out, the mind becomes rightly and instantly dissolved into nonconceptuality.
intent_summary: Use a vast or dizzying spatial setting to break conceptual thought and dissolve the mind into emptiness.
beginner_explanation: Looking into a deep well or from a great height can suddenly quiet thinking because the mind loses its usual footing. The verse uses that shock to point beyond thought. In that openness, the mind can drop into a simple, wordless awareness.
scholar_explanation: The external abyss serves as an upāya for internal avikalpa, because the destabilization of spatial reference can precipitate cittalaya. The term mahāgate suggests an expansive or abyssal opening, and the key result is avikalpa-mati, nonconceptual cognition. This is a well-known VBT technique: an external spatial perception mirrors and induces inward dissolution.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Mind Everywhere
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत िाह्ये िाभ्यन्तरेऽवप वा ।
ति ति वशिािास्था व्यापकत्वात्क्व यास्यवत ॥ ११६ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra mano yāvat bāhye nābhyantare api vā |
tatra tatra śivāvasthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati || 116 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes, outside or also within, there is the state of Śiva; because of its all-pervasiveness, where could it go?
intent_summary: Recognize that Śiva-consciousness pervades every mental movement, leaving nowhere outside it to go.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that wherever your mind wanders, you are still inside the same vast awareness. There is no place outside consciousness, whether the thought feels inward or outward. This can help you stop feeling that you must chase spiritual experience somewhere else.
scholar_explanation: The verse states śivāvasthā as vyāpakatva, all-pervasiveness: every movement of mano is already within the field of Śiva. The rhetorical question “kva yāsyati” dissolves the illusion of departure and destination. This is a direct nondual recognition teaching, stressing that spatial and psychical distinctions do not escape the ground of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Trace Consciousness to Its Source
sanskrit:
यि यिाक्षमागेण चैतन्यं व्यज्यते विभो् ।
तस्य तन्मािधवमधत्वावच्चल्लयाद्भवरतात्मता ॥ ११७ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra akṣamārgeṇa caitanyaṃ vyajyate vibhoḥ |
tasya tanmātradharmatvāc cittalayo bhavet || 117 ||
translation: Wherever, through any sense-channel, consciousness manifests, by following that reality as only that single quality, the mind dissolves.
intent_summary: Follow any sensory emergence of consciousness back to its pure, simple essence until thought dissolves.
beginner_explanation: Any time awareness appears through sight, hearing, touch, or another sense, you can use that moment as a doorway inward. Instead of getting lost in the object, notice the pure knowing itself. If you stay with that bare presence, the busy mind can fall away.
scholar_explanation: Akṣamārga indicates the sensory pathways, and caitanya vyajyate marks the manifesting of consciousness in perception. By attending to its tanmātra-dharma, the bare modality or essential quality, one reaches cittalaya. The method teaches that perception itself, stripped of conceptual overlay, leads back to the universal consciousness of Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Breakthrough in Fear and Hunger
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्षुताद्यन्ते भये शोके गह्वरे वा रणाद्द्रुते ।
कुतूहलेक्षुधाद्यन्ते ब्रह्मसत्तामयी दशा ॥ ११८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
kṣutādyante bhaye śoke gahvare vā raṇād drute |
kutūhalekṣudhādyante brahmasattāmayī daśā || 118 ||
translation: At the end of hunger and other such states, in fear, sorrow, in a cave, or when fleeing from battle, at the end of curiosity and hunger, there is a state filled with the presence of Brahman.
intent_summary: Use intense emotional or physiological thresholds as openings into a Brahman-filled state.
beginner_explanation: Strong feelings like fear, grief, hunger, or sudden curiosity can shake you out of ordinary habits. This verse says those charged moments can also reveal a deeper presence if you notice them carefully. Instead of resisting the intensity, you can use it as a doorway to awareness.
scholar_explanation: The verse groups liminal states—kṣut, bhaya, śoka, and even the cave-like isolation of gahvara—as thresholds where brahmasattā may shine. The end-state is not ordinary calm but a Brahman-pervaded condition arising precisely when habitual affect is interrupted. This reflects the Tantra’s use of affective extremity as a catalyst for recognition (pratyabhijñā).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Release the Ground Under the Body
sanskrit:
वस्तुषु स्मयधमाणेषु दृष्टे देशे मनस् त्यजेत् ।
स्वशरीरं निराधारं कृत्वा प्रसरवत् प्रभुः ॥ ११९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
vastuṣu smaryamāṇeṣu dṛṣṭe deśe manas tyajet |
svaśarīraṃ nirādhāraṃ kṛtvā prasarat prabhuḥ || 119 ||
translation: When objects are being remembered, in the seen place, one should abandon the mind; making one’s own body supportless, the Lord expands.
intent_summary: Let go of mental fixation on objects and sense the body as unsupported so awareness can widen freely.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to stop leaning mentally on things you are remembering or seeing. Then, instead of feeling like a solid body sitting on the ground, imagine that the body has no support. In that loosened state, awareness can feel spacious and expansive.
scholar_explanation: The practice suspends manas from vastu-smaraṇa and dṛṣṭa-deśa, sensory and memorial objectivity. By rendering the body nirādhāra, supportless, one experiences the prabhutva, expansiveness or lordship, of awareness itself. The verse aligns bodily de-centering with the nondual recognition that the self is not limited by physical support.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting the Mind in the Void
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
क्ववचद्वस्तुवन विन्यस्य शनैदृधवष्टम् वनितधयेत् ।
तज्ज्ञानं वचत्तसवहतं देवि शून्यालयो भवेत् ॥१२० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanai dṛṣṭiṃ vinirgatām |
taj jñānaṃ cittasahitaṃ devi śūnyālayaṃ bhavet || 120 ||
translation: Fixing the gaze slowly on some object, let the sight go outward; then, O Devi, that knowledge together with the mind becomes a dwelling in emptiness.
intent_summary: Let the gaze settle gently on an object and then move beyond it so cognition abides in emptiness.
beginner_explanation: This method uses a simple object as a stepping stone. You look steadily, then allow the act of seeing to move past the object, as if awareness is passing through a window into open space. The result is a quiet inner emptiness that can hold both mind and knowing.
scholar_explanation: The dṛṣṭi is first vinyasya on a vastu, then made vinirgatā, outward-going yet transcended. The end-state, śūnyālaya, is a “dwelling in emptiness” where citta and jñāna are no longer split from their ground. This technique demonstrates how external form can be used to induce a stable interior void, not nihilism but luminous śūnyatā.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Devotional Overflow into Śakti
sanskrit:
भक्त्युद्रेकावद्वरिस्य यादृशी जायते मवत् ।
सा शवि् शाङ्करी वनत्यं भियेत्तां तत् वशि् ॥ १२१ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktyudrekāvadvarisya yādṛśī jāyate mavat |
 sā śaviḥ śāṅkarī vanatyaṃ bhiyettāṃ tat vaśiḥ || 121 ||
translation: As that state arises from an overflow of devotion, so does the power of Śaṅkarī become established; by that one becomes governed by that power.
intent_summary: Use intense devotion to let the divine power of consciousness arise and take over the practitioner.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when devotion becomes strong enough, a special inner power awakens. Instead of forcing progress, you let heartfelt devotion draw you into a deeper state. The practice is to love the divine so fully that your whole being is transformed by it.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to bhakti-udreka, an intensified surge of devotion, as a trigger for śakti to become manifest and stable. The “power of Śaṅkarī” here suggests the dynamic aspect of consciousness that carries the practitioner beyond ordinary agency. This aligns with VBT’s recognition that emotional intensification can function as a direct upāya when it ripens into absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Emptying the Middle Space
sanskrit:
िस्त्वन्तरे िेद्यमाने सिधिस्तुषु शून्यता ।
तामेि मनसा ध्यात्वा विवदतोऽवप प्रशाम्यवत ॥ १२२ ॥
transliteration:
hastvantare vedyamāne sidhistuṣu śūnyatā |
 tāmeva manasā dhyātvā vividato'pi praśāmyati || 122 ||
translation: When emptiness is apprehended in the interval between the hands, or in the midst of the supports, by meditating on that alone with the mind, even one who is bewildered becomes pacified.
intent_summary: Focus on the empty interval or gap between things to settle the mind into stillness.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the quiet space between two things, like the gap between the hands or between supports. If you rest attention on that empty interval, the mind naturally calms down. It is like noticing the silence between sounds instead of chasing the sounds themselves.
scholar_explanation: The instruction uses śūnyatā in the “between” (antara) as a contemplative support, echoing VBT’s interest in liminal intervals and akhaṇḍa awareness. By dhyāna on that void-like gap, even a distracted (vividata) mind is pacified, indicating that emptiness is not mere negation but a doorway to stabilized consciousness. This sits near other gap-practices in the Tantra where the interval becomes the locus of revelation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Purity Beyond Pure and Impure
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वकंवचज्ज्ञैयाध स्मृता शुवद्ध् सा शुवद्ध् शम्भुदशधने ।
न शुवचह्यधशुवचस्तस्मावन्नविधकल्प् सुखी भवेत् ॥ १२३ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
kiṃcijjñeyā smṛtā śuddhiḥ sā śuddhiḥ śambhudarśane |
na śucirhy aśucis tasmān nirvikalpaḥ sukī bhavet || 123 ||
translation: What is remembered as a little knowable purity—such purity is in the vision of Śambhu; therefore, neither pure nor impure, one becomes happy, free from conceptual construction.
intent_summary: Recognize that real purity lies in direct vision of Śiva, beyond social or mental judgments of pure and impure.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that ordinary ideas of clean and unclean are limited. A deeper purity comes from seeing reality directly, without mental labels. When you stop dividing the world into rigid categories, a simpler happiness appears.
scholar_explanation: The verse distinguishes conventional śuddhi from śuddhi in śambhu-darśana, implying that true purity is ontological rather than ritualistic. The final phrase, nirvikalpaḥ, indicates freedom from conceptual partitioning, so the practitioner rests in nondual awareness where śuci/aśuci lose force. This is a classic VBT move: transcending dualistic evaluation by seeing all from the standpoint of Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava in All Perceptions
sanskrit:
सिधि भैरवो भाि् सामान्येष्ववप गोचर् ।
न च तद्व्यवतरेिेण परोऽस्तीत्यद्वया गवत् ॥ १२४ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ bhairavo bhāvः sāmānyeṣv api gocaraḥ |
na ca tadvyatirekeṇa paro'stīty advayā gatiḥ || 124 ||
translation: Bhairava is the nature of all, and he is present even in ordinary perceptions; apart from that, there is no other reality—this is the movement of nonduality.
intent_summary: See Bhairava as the essence present in every ordinary experience, with nothing existing outside that unity.
beginner_explanation: This verse teaches that the divine is not only in special mystical experiences. It is present in everyday things too. If you look closely, you can learn to see the same one reality everywhere.
scholar_explanation: Bhairava is declared sarva-bhāva, the being/nature of all phenomena, accessible even through sāmānya-go-carāḥ, ordinary fields of experience. The denial of anything “other” (para) outside of that is a direct articulation of advayā gati, the nondual trajectory of the text. This verse functions as a doctrinal anchor for the subsequent contemplations on equality, emptiness, and freedom from attraction/aversion.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Equalizing Honor and Dishonor
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सम् शिौ च वमिे च समो मानािमानयो् ॥
ब्रह्मण् पवरपूणधत्वावदवत ज्ञात्वा सुखी भवेत् ॥ १२५ ॥
transliteration:
samaṃ śatrau ca mitre ca samo mānāvamānayoḥ ||
brahmaṇaḥ paripūrṇatvād iti jñātvā sukī bhavet || 125 ||
translation: One who is equal toward enemy and friend, and equal toward honor and dishonor, knowing this through the full completeness of Brahman, becomes happy.
intent_summary: Cultivate inner equality so praise and blame, friend and foe, do not disturb the sense of completeness.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to stay balanced whether people treat you well or badly. When you know yourself as already complete, praise and insult lose their power. It is like standing in a strong center while waves come and go around you.
scholar_explanation: The practice is sāmatva, equanimity toward śatrau/mitre and māna/avamāna, grounded in Brahman’s paripūrṇatva, its fullness or plenitude. This is not moral indifference but a nonreactive absorption into completeness, consistent with the text’s repeated collapse of opposites into awareness. The verse complements the more affective and cognitive methods by showing that equanimity itself can disclose Brahman.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Attraction and Aversion
sanskrit:
न द्वेषं भाियेत्क्वावप न रागं भाियेत्क्ववचत् ।
रागद्वेषविवनमुधिौ मध्ये ब्रह्म प्रसपधवत ॥ १२६ ॥
transliteration:
na dveṣaṃ bhāvayet kvāpi na rāgaṃ bhāvayet kvacit |
 rāgadveṣavininmuktau madhye brahma prasarpati || 126 ||
translation: One should not foster aversion anywhere, nor foster attachment anywhere; when free from attachment and aversion, Brahman expands in the middle.
intent_summary: Release both craving and rejection so the middle state of Brahman can reveal itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says not to feed either liking or dislike. If you stop pushing and pulling, a deeper stillness opens up. In that stillness, you can sense a larger reality that was hidden by your reactions.
scholar_explanation: Rāga and dveṣa are the classic twin disturbances of consciousness; their renunciation enables entry into the madhya, the central nondual interval. The verb prasarpati suggests Brahman as spontaneously pervading once affective polarization ceases. This verse is closely related to the VBT’s “middle” practices, where the center is not a point but a condition of uncontrived lucidity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating Bhairava in All
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
यदिेद्यं यदग्राह्यं यच्छून्यं यदभािगम् ।
तत्सिं भैरवं भाव्यं तदन्ते िोधसम्भि् ॥ १२७ ॥
transliteration:
yadvedyaṃ yadagrāhyaṃ yacchūnyaṃ yadabhāvagam |
 tat sarvaṃ bhairavaṃ bhāvyaṃ tadante bodhasambhavaḥ || 127 ||
translation: Whatever is knowable, whatever is ungraspable, whatever is empty, whatever is beyond existence—one should contemplate all that as Bhairava; then at the end knowledge arises.
intent_summary: See every mode of experience, including emptiness and the ungraspable, as Bhairava until direct knowing arises.
beginner_explanation: This verse invites you to regard everything as the divine: what you can know, what you cannot grasp, even emptiness itself. Instead of separating sacred from ordinary, you train the mind to see the same presence in all. In that way, understanding can suddenly bloom on its own.
scholar_explanation: The verse universalizes bhāvanā by including vedya, agrāhya, śūnya, and abhāvagata within Bhairava’s scope. This is a sophisticated nondual instruction: even absence and ungraspability are not outside the divine, but modalities through which bodha (awakening/knowledge) emerges. It echoes the text’s strategy of totalizing perception until conceptual exclusivity collapses.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolving into Sky-like Space
sanskrit:
वनत्ये वनराश्रये शून्ये व्यापके कलनोविते ।
िाह्याकाशे मनः कृत्वा वनराकाशं समाविशेत् ॥ १२८ ॥
transliteration:
nitye nirāśraye śūnye vyāpake kalanodite |
 bāhyākāśe manaḥ kṛtvā nirākāśaṃ samāviśet || 128 ||
translation: In the eternal, unsupported, empty, all-pervading, and manifestly luminous, placing the mind in external space, one should enter into spacelessness.
intent_summary: Use the vastness of outer space as a doorway to realize a boundless inner space beyond all reference points.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests looking into open space and letting the mind merge with its vastness. Then, instead of staying fixed on objects, you enter a more open state with no boundaries. It is like gazing into the sky until the mind becomes sky-like too.
scholar_explanation: The instruction moves from bāhya-ākāśa, outer space, to nir-ākāśa, spacelessness, a common Tantric paradox where contemplation of space leads beyond spatialization. The descriptors nitya, nirāśraya, śūnya, and vyāpaka frame the absolute as unsupported, empty, and all-pervasive, while kalanodita suggests it is also manifest to discernment. This practice is related to the VBT’s space contemplations where the outer mirror becomes a threshold to consciousness itself.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Following the Mind to Its End
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत तत्तत् तेनैि तत्क्षणम् ।
पवरत्यज्यानिवस्थत्या वनस्तरङ्गस्ततो भवेत् ॥ १२९ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra mano yāti tat tat tenaiva tatkṣaṇam |
 parityajyānavasthityā nistaraṅgas tato bhavet || 129 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes, right there and then one should abandon it; by not allowing it to remain, one becomes wave-less.
intent_summary: Interrupt every mental movement immediately so the mind settles into a calm, wave-free state.
beginner_explanation: This verse tells you not to follow every thought. The moment the mind moves, let it go and do not hold onto it. Over time, the inner surface becomes still, like water with no waves.
scholar_explanation: The method is a radical de-identification with manas: wherever it goes, it is abandoned in the same instant, preventing fixation and continuity of vṛtti. The result is nistaraṅga, wave-lessness, a classic image for dissolved mental fluctuation and emergent samādhi. This is a practical complement to the previous verses on space and the middle, converting insight into immediate non-clinging.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Continuous Repetition of Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
भया सिधम् रियवत सिधदो व्यापकोऽवखले ।
इवत भैरवशब्दस्य सन्ततोच्चारणावच्छि् ॥ १३० ॥
transliteration:
bhayā sarvaṃ riṣayati sarvado vyāpako'khile |
 iti bhairavaśabdasya santatoccāraṇāvacchit || 130 ||
translation: By fear, everything is shaken; the giver of all is all-pervading throughout the whole. Thus, by uninterrupted utterance of the word 'Bhairava'...
