intent_summary: Use continuous repetition of the sacred name Bhairava to saturate awareness and transform fear into all-pervading presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to repeating the word “Bhairava” again and again. The sound of the name helps keep the mind connected to the divine and can soften fear. It is like holding a strong, steady rhythm that carries you inward.
scholar_explanation: Although the OCR is damaged, the verse clearly refers to santata-uccāraṇa of the bhairava-śabda, continuous utterance of the name as a sonic upāya. The opening mention of bhaya suggests that fear is overcome by invoking the all-pervasive donor or ground of all, turning mantra into a direct support for presence. This verse belongs to the sound/mantra strand of VBT where repetition is not merely devotional but a means of stabilization and identity with Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Through the 'I' and 'Mine'
sanskrit:
अहं ममेदवमत्यावद प्रवतपवत्तप्रसङ्गत् ।
वनराधारे मनो यावत तद्ध्यानप्रेरणाच्छमी ॥ १३१ ॥
transliteration:
ahaṃ mamedam ity āvad pravṛtti-prasaṅgāt |
nirādhāre mano yāvat tad dhyāna-preraṇāc chami || 131 ||
translation: As long as the mind runs on in the movement of 'I' and 'mine,' remain steady by directing meditation that leads it back to the supportless state.
intent_summary: To dissolve possessiveness and egoic self-reference by returning the mind to its supportless source through meditation.
beginner_explanation: This verse points out that the mind keeps getting pulled into thoughts of “me” and “mine.” Instead of following those thoughts, you are asked to gently bring attention back to a place with no grasping or support. It is like letting a ball stop bouncing and settle into stillness.
scholar_explanation: The verse critiques ahaṃ-mama-vṛtti, the egoic appropriation that sustains saṃsāric identification. The phrase nirādhāre mano yāvat suggests abiding until mind loses its prop-support and collapses into its own source through dhyāna-preraṇā. In Kashmir Śaivism this aligns with recognition of the unconstructed field beyond vikalpa, where subject-object appropriation ceases.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the All-Pervading Support
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
वनत्यो विभुवनधराधारो व्यापकश्चावखलावधप् ।
शब्दान्प्रवतक्षणं ध्यायन्कृताथोऽथाधनुरूपत् ॥ १३२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
niḥśeṣaṃ viśva-bhuvana-dharādhāro vyāpakaś cākhila-āvadhāḥ |
śabdān pravṛtta-kṣaṇaṃ dhyāyan kṛtārtho 'tha dhānurūpataḥ || 132 ||
translation: The support of the entire world of worlds is the all-pervading one, whose limits are nowhere. Meditating on sounds at the instant they arise, one becomes fulfilled and assumes the nature of the bow.
intent_summary: To recognize the all-pervading ground of reality and use attention on arising sound as a means of entering completeness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that reality is supported by something vast and everywhere-present, with no real boundary. If you watch a sound right at the moment it appears, your awareness can open into that boundless background. The “bow” image suggests a poised, focused practice, like drawing a bow before release.
scholar_explanation: The verse identifies the dharādhāra as the vyāpaka, limitless substratum of the viśva-bhuvana, echoing Śiva as sarvavyāpī. The practice is śabdān pravṛtta-kṣaṇam dhyāyan: catching sound at its inception, where differentiation has not yet solidified, thus enabling kṛtārthatva. The concluding dhānurūpataḥ is textually uncertain but likely indicates a collected, tensile alignment of consciousness, akin to upāya through nāda.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Holding the World as Magical Appearance
sanskrit:
अतत्त्ववमन्द्रजालाभवमदं सिधमिवस्थतम् ।
वकं तत्त्ववमन्द्रजालस्य इवत दार्ढ्ाधच्छमं व्रजेत् ॥ १३३ ॥
transliteration:
atattva-mandra-jālābhaṃ idaṃ siddham iva sthitam |
kvaṃ tattva-mandra-jālasya iti dārḍhyāc chamaṃ vrajet || 133 ||
translation: This appears like a subtle net of illusion, yet it stands as if already accomplished. Understanding the subtle net of reality in this way, one should go to peace through firmness.
intent_summary: To see the world as a subtle, magical appearance and thereby settle into peace without clinging to appearances as ultimate.
beginner_explanation: The verse compares experience to a delicate net of illusion: real enough to appear, but not something to cling to as solid. When you understand that appearances are like this, you can relax instead of fighting or grasping them. The result is a calmer and steadier mind.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of mandra-jāla evokes māyā-like appearance, while siddham iva sthitam indicates the world’s seeming accomplishedness without ultimate substantiality. The instruction is to inquire into the status of tattva and the subtle web of manifestation, then rest in śama through dārḍhya, firm insight. This resonates with nondual Śaiva views that the universe is a real but dependent self-display of consciousness, not an independently existing object-world.

speaker: Bhairava
title: World as Empty of Inherent Fixity
sanskrit:
आत्मनो वनविधकारस्य क्व ज्ञानं क्व च वा वक्रया ।
ज्ञानायत्ता िवहभाधिा अत् शून्यवमदं जगत् ॥ १३४ ॥
transliteration:
ātmano nividha-kārasya kva jñānaṃ kva ca vā kriyā |
jñānāyattā vihabhāṣā at śūnyam idaṃ jagat || 134 ||
translation: For the self, which is of many forms, where is knowledge and where is action? Since speech and cognition depend on knowing, this world is empty.
intent_summary: To perceive that knowing, acting, and the world itself lack independent essence and arise within awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to look for a fixed “self” behind experience and find that it cannot be pinned down. If even knowledge, action, and speech depend on awareness, then the world is not a solid thing standing on its own. Seeing this can make experience feel open and spacious rather than rigid.
scholar_explanation: The verse deconstructs the apparent autonomy of jñāna, kriyā, and speech by locating them within the multiplicity of the self’s manifestations, which are ultimately non-self-subsisting. The claim that idaṃ jagat is śūnyam does not imply nihilism but the absence of svabhāva, aligning with the Śaiva insight that phenomena are dependent expressions of consciousness. It points the practitioner toward a recognition of awareness as the ground in which epistemic and active functions arise.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Beyond Bondage and Liberation
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
न मे बन्धो न मोक्षो मे भीतस्यैता विभीषिकाः ।
प्रवर्तविम्बवमदम् शुद्धेजडरेष्विव विवस्वत् ॥ १३५ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
na me bandho na mokṣo me bhītasyaitā vibhīṣikāḥ |
pravṛtti-bimbam idam śuddhe jḍareṣv iva vivasvat || 135 ||
translation: For me there is no bondage and no liberation; these are terrors for the fearful. This is but a reflection of activity, like the sun in pure waters.
intent_summary: To transcend fear-based ideas of bondage and liberation by resting in the ever-free nature of consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that bondage and liberation are labels that can scare the mind, but they do not define the deepest reality. What you experience as life’s ups and downs are like the sun reflected in clear water: vivid, yet not the sun itself. The practice is to see through the reflection and rest in what does not change.
scholar_explanation: The statement na me bandho na mokṣo me rejects dualistic soteriology from the standpoint of the ever-free Bhairava, where bondage and release are vibhīṣikā, fear-producing constructs. Pravṛtti-bimbam idam frames phenomenal processes as mere reflection, comparable to the sun in clear water—appearing without compromising the source. This is a classic nondual Śaiva declaration that liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā), not acquisition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Withdrawing the Senses to Rest in Self
sanskrit:
इन्द्रियद्वारकं सर्वं सुखदुःखावदसम्गमम् ।
इतीन्द्रियाणि सम्त्यज्य स्वस्थः स्वात्मनि वर्तते ॥ १३६ ॥
transliteration:
indriya-dvārakaṃ sarvaṃ sukha-duḥkhādi-saṃgamam |
ity indriyāṇi saṃtyajya svasthaḥ svātmani vartate || 136 ||
translation: Everything comes through the gateways of the senses and is joined with pleasure and pain. Therefore, abandoning the senses, one abides established in oneself.
intent_summary: To step back from sensory involvement so awareness can rest in its own native stability.
beginner_explanation: This verse reminds you that most of your ups and downs enter through the senses: sights, sounds, touches, and so on. If you temporarily stop chasing them, you can notice a quieter place inside that is already steady. It is like closing a noisy window so you can hear the room itself.
scholar_explanation: The senses are presented as indriya-dvāra, gateways through which sukha-duḥkha and their associated oscillations enter the psyche. By saṃtyajya indriyāṇi, the practitioner does not reject embodiment but dis-identifies from sensory capture and becomes svastha, स्थापित in svātman. This corresponds to pratyāhāra-like interiorization, but here it serves immediate recognition of the self-luminous ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: One Light of Knowing and Known
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
ज्ञानप्रकाशकं सर्वेणात्मा प्रकाशकः ।
एकवमकस्वभावत्वात्ज्ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं विभाव्यते ॥ १३७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
jñāna-prakāśakaṃ sarvaṃ ātma prakāśakaḥ |
ekātmakasvabhāvatvāj jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ vibhāvyate || 137 ||
translation: The self is the illuminator of all that illuminates knowledge. Because it has the nature of being one, knowledge and the known are imagined as distinct.
intent_summary: To recognize that the self is the single light by which both knowing and objects known appear.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that awareness is like the light that makes everything visible, including thoughts and ideas. Without that light, nothing could be known at all. The seeming split between the knower and the thing known is something the mind adds.
scholar_explanation: Ātma is described as jñāna-prakāśaka, the illumination underlying all epistemic events, while ekātmakasvabhāva undermines the jñāta-jñeya bifurcation. The verse presents duality as vibhāvanā, conceptual superimposition, on the basis of the one self-luminous consciousness. It is a direct articulation of the Pratyabhijñā insight that cognition is self-revealing and non-dual in its essence.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Fourfold Nature Fades into Bhairava
sanskrit:
मानसं चेतना शक्तिरात्मा चेति चतुष्टयम् ।
यदा प्रिये पवरक्षीणं तदा तद्भैरवं वपुः ॥ १३८ ॥
transliteration:
mānasaṃ cetanā śaktir ātmā ceti catuṣṭayam |
yadā priye pari-kṣīṇaṃ tadā tad bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 138 ||
translation: Mind, awareness, power, and self: this fourfold set, when fully exhausted, O beloved, becomes the body of Bhairava.
intent_summary: To dissolve the fourfold structure of ordinary experience so the practitioner recognizes the totality as Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Here the text lists the main pieces of ordinary experience—mind, awareness, energy, and self. When their separate feeling is worn out or dissolved, what remains is not emptiness in a negative sense but the living reality of Bhairava. It is like realizing that many waves are really just one ocean.
scholar_explanation: The catuṣṭaya of mānasa, cetanā, śakti, and ātma represents the functional differentiation through which ordinary subjectivity operates. When these are pari-kṣīṇa, the distinctions collapse and the practitioner apprehends the total field as Bhairava-vapus, the body of nondual consciousness. This is a culminating recognition formula consistent with the VBT’s repeated movement from analytic disclosure to total identification.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Hundred Teachings and the Beyond
sanskrit:
वनस्तरङ्गोपदेशानां शतमुक्तं समासत् ।
द्वादशाभ्यवधकं देवि यज्ज्ञात्वा ज्ञानविज्जन् ॥ १३९ ॥
transliteration:
nirantaraṅga-upadeśānāṃ śatam uktaṃ samāsataḥ |
dvādaśābhyadhikaṃ devi yaj jñātvā jñāna-vij jayet || 139 ||
translation: Thus, O Devi, a hundred continuous teachings have been briefly spoken. Knowing what is beyond the twelve, one becomes a knower of knowledge.
intent_summary: To conclude the teaching by affirming the completeness of the methods and pointing beyond them to direct knowledge.
beginner_explanation: This verse signals that many teachings have been given in summary form. But it also says that real understanding comes from seeing what lies beyond the twelve—meaning beyond fixed counts, categories, or methods. The point is to move from listening to direct realization.
scholar_explanation: The verse summarizes the upadeśa as śata, a hundred instructions, while also invoking a dvādaśābhyadhika dimension—textually and interpretively opaque but likely indicating transcendence of enumerated methods or states. Jñāna-vij suggests one who has mastered or embodied gnosis, not merely conceptually but experientially. It serves as a metatextual hinge from the dhāraṇās toward their consummation in immediate insight.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Becoming Bhairava Through Union
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
अि चैकतमे युिो जायते भैरवः स्वयम् ।
वाचा करोति कर्माणि शापानुग्रहकारकः ॥ १४० ॥
transliteration:
vijñāna-bhairava-tantram |
athaikatame yukto jāyate bhairavaḥ svayam |
vācā karoti karmāṇi śāpānugraha-kārakaḥ || 140 ||
translation: Then, when united in the one, one becomes Bhairava himself. Through speech he performs actions as one who grants curses and blessings.
intent_summary: To indicate that complete union in singular consciousness makes one identical with Bhairava, whose speech becomes potent expression.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when you become firmly established in the one reality, you are not separate from Bhairava. In that state, even speech becomes powerful and effective, able to bless or to cut through confusion. It suggests a life lived from direct unity rather than ego.
scholar_explanation: Yukta in the aikatama denotes absorption into the one nondual reality, at which point the practitioner does not merely resemble but is jāyate bhairavaḥ svayam. Speech (vāc) becomes śāpa-anugraha-kāraka, indicating the transformed efficacy of vāṇī when issued from realized unity. This reflects the Śaiva ideal of siddha speech rooted in identity with the supreme.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Immortality through Yogic Powers
sanskrit:
अजरामरतामेति सोऽणिमादिगुणान्वित् ।
योगिनीनां प्रियो देवि सिद्धमेलापकाधिपः ॥ १४१ ॥
transliteration:
ajarāmaratām eti so'ṇimādi-guṇānvitaḥ |
yoginīnāṃ priyo devi siddha-melāpakādhipaḥ || 141 ||
translation: He attains deathlessness and immortality, endowed with the powers beginning with aṇimā. He becomes dear to the yoginīs, O Devi, the lord of the gathering of siddhas.
intent_summary: Bhairava describes the exalted state and powers that arise when realization ripens into perfected siddha-status.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that some spiritual attainment is linked with extraordinary abilities and a state beyond ordinary aging and death. It also says such a person becomes attractive to advanced yogic beings and masters. In simple terms, realization is portrayed as a life transformed beyond normal limits.
scholar_explanation: This is a descriptive, concluding-style verse glorifying siddhi-bearing realization: aṇimā and the other ādi-guṇas point to the aṣṭa-siddhis. Ajarāmaratva indicates transcendence of ordinary bodily limitation, while yoginī-priya and siddha-melāpaka-adhipa evoke the tantric circle of accomplished beings. The verse belongs more to the doctrinal celebration of attainment than to a dhāraṇā instruction.

speaker: Devi
title: Freedom Beyond Action
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
जीन्नवप विमुक्तोऽसौ कुर्वन्नवप न वलप्यते ।
इदं यवद विपुदेव परायाश्च महेश्वर ॥ १४२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
jīnnava pa vimukto'sau kurvann ava pa na valapyate |
idam yavad vipudeva parāyāś ca maheśvara || 142 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. He is liberated, and though acting, he is not afflicted. This is so, O great Lord, up to the supreme state of the divine.
intent_summary: Devi asks about the liberated one who remains untouched by action, pointing toward effortless freedom in activity.
beginner_explanation: The verse asks how someone can be free even while still doing things in the world. It suggests that true liberation is not about stopping all action, but about being inwardly untouched by it. Think of someone playing a role without getting lost in the role.
scholar_explanation: Despite OCR disturbance, the semantic thrust is clear: mukta yet karma-kṛt, untouched by the binding force of action. This reflects the Tantric nondual idea of jīvanmukti, where the liberated one acts without kartṛtva-abhimāna. The phrase parāyāś ca maheśvara signals the ascent toward Parā, the supreme शक्ति/awareness beyond duality.

speaker: Devi
title: Who Is the Ritual Doer?
sanskrit:
एवमुिव्यवस्थायां जप्यते को जपश्च कः ।
ध्यायते को महानाथ पूज्यते कश्च तृप्यति ॥ १४३ ॥
transliteration:
evam uvyavasthāyāṃ japyate ko japaś ca kaḥ |
dhyāyate ko mahānātha pūjyate kash ca tṛpyati || 143 ||
translation: In such a condition, who is it that recites, and what is recitation? Who meditates, O Great Lord, who is worshiped, and who is satisfied?
intent_summary: Devi probes the collapse of subject-object distinctions in the highest realization, where ritual roles lose their footing.
beginner_explanation: Here the question is: if everything is ultimately one, who is doing the chanting or meditation? The verse points to a state where the usual idea of “me doing practice” starts to dissolve. It asks whether worship itself makes sense when there is no separate self left.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic nondual interrogation of ritual and agency: japa, dhyāna, pūjā, and tṛpti presuppose distinct agent, act, and object. Devi’s question challenges the conventional triad within the paramārtha of Bhairava, anticipating the later verse that collapses homa, yāga, and japa into consciousness itself. It aligns with the VBT’s recurring move from external practice to immediate recognition (pratyabhijñā-like insight).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Rituals as Outer Practices
sanskrit:
हूयते कस्य वा होमो यागः कस्य च किं कथम् ।
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
एषाि प्रवक्रया िाह्या स्थूलेष्वेि मृगेक्षणे ॥ १४४ ॥
transliteration:
hūyate kasya vā homo yāgaḥ kasya ca kiṃ katham |
vijñānabhairava tantram
eṣā hi pravaktṛkā bāhyā sthūleṣv eva mṛgekṣaṇe || 144 ||
translation: For whom is the oblation offered, and whose is the sacrifice, and how? Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. O deer-eyed one, this teaching is indeed external, pertaining only to gross things.
intent_summary: Bhairava explains that ordinary sacrificial ritual belongs to the outer, gross level and is not the highest truth.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that ritual actions like offering into fire belong to the outer level of practice. It’s as if Bhairava is saying, “That’s useful, but it’s not the deepest layer.” The deeper meaning is inward, not just physical.
scholar_explanation: Homa and yāga are here relegated to bāhya and sthūla—external and gross—relative to the subtle internalization central to this tantra. The verse critiques literalistic ritual by implying that its true significance lies in inner recognition rather than material performance. It prepares for the following verses, where japa, dhyāna, and pūjā are redefined as resonance, awareness, and pure spaciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mantra as Inner Sound
sanskrit:
भूयो भूय् परे भावे भावना भाव्यते वह या ।
जप् सोऽि स्वयं नादो मन्त्रात्मा जप्य ईदृश् ॥ १४५ ॥
transliteration:
bhūyo bhūyaḥ pare bhāve bhāvanā bhāvyate yā |
japaḥ so'yaṃ svayaṃ nādo mantra-ātmā japyā īdṛśī || 145 ||
translation: Again and again, in the supreme state, the contemplation that is contemplated—this very japa is itself the spontaneous sound (nāda), having the essence of mantra; such is the recitation.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that true mantra practice is the repeated return to the supreme state, where recitation becomes spontaneous inner sound.
beginner_explanation: Instead of chanting words mechanically, this verse points to a deeper kind of mantra that becomes an inner vibration. When attention rests in the highest state again and again, the practice itself turns into a natural hum or current inside. The sound is not just spoken; it is lived.
scholar_explanation: The verse reinterprets japa as nāda—self-arising sonic presence—within pare bhāva, the supreme condition. Bhāvanā becomes reflexive: the contemplative act is itself what is contemplated, collapsing the distinction between means and goal. This is central to VBT’s inward mantra- सिद्धि, where mantra-ātman is not phonetic repetition alone but awakened resonance.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Formless Steady Meditation
sanskrit:
ध्यानं वह वनश्चला िुवद्धवनधराकारा वनराश्रया ।
न तु ध्यानं शरीरावक्षमुखहस्तावदकल्पना ॥ १४६ ॥
transliteration:
dhyānaṃ hi niścalā buddhir nirākārā nirāśrayā |
na tu dhyānaṃ śarīrāvakṣa-mukha-hastādi-kalpanā || 146 ||
translation: Meditation is the unmoving intellect, formless and without support; meditation is not an imagination of the chest, face, hands, and so on of the body.
intent_summary: The verse defines meditation as nonconceptual, formless stability rather than visualizing bodily images.
beginner_explanation: Meditation here is described as a steady mind that doesn’t cling to pictures or props. It is not about making up an image of the body or forcing the mind to imagine shapes. Instead, it is about resting in clear, still awareness.
scholar_explanation: Dhyāna is defined apophatically as niścalā buddhiḥ, nirākārā, nirāśrayā—stable cognition without form or support. The verse explicitly rejects bodily visualization (śarīrāvakṣa-mukha-hasta-kalpanā) as the essence of meditation, contrasting internal stillness with object-based visualization. This resonates with the VBT’s emphasis on immediate awareness over constructed mental imagery.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Worship in Infinite Space
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
पूजा नाम न पुष्पाद्यैर्यथा मवत्यते दृढा ।
वनविधकल्पे महाव्योमि सा पूजा ह्यद्राल्लयः ॥ १४७ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
pūjā nāma na puṣpādyair yathā manyate dṛḍhā |
nivikalpe mahāvyome sā pūjā hy adhrāl layaḥ || 147 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. Worship is not, as it is commonly thought, with flowers and the like. In the great sky of nonconceptual awareness, that alone is worship; there is truly dissolution into the supportless.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that true worship is absorption in vast, thought-free awareness rather than external offerings.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that real worship is not mainly about flowers or objects. The deepest offering is entering a huge inner openness where thoughts settle down. In that openness, the feeling of separation melts away.
scholar_explanation: Pūjā is redefined as being established in the mahā-vyoma of nivikalpa—nondual, nonconceptual spaciousness. The verse shifts from external ritual implements (puṣpa-ādi) to inner immersion, and identifies worship with laya into the supportless (adhrāl), echoing the tantra’s repeated internalization of ritual. This is a key example of ritual transmutation in the VBT.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Satisfaction in Ever-New Modes
sanskrit:
अनेकतमयुविस्थे योत्पद्येत वदनावद्दनम् ।
भवरताकारता साऽव तृप्तिरत्यन्तपूर्णता ॥ १४८ ॥
transliteration:
anekatamayukṣṭe yotpadyeta dinādinam |
bharatākāratā sā ca tṛptir atyantapūrṇatā || 148 ||
translation: Whatever arises day after day in the midst of many modes, that very state of fullness is satisfaction and utter plenitude.
intent_summary: The verse points to a fullness that remains present amid changing experiences, producing deep contentment.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that when life keeps changing in many ways, a deeper fullness can still remain. That fullness is not dependent on getting one particular experience. It feels like being completely satisfied from within.
scholar_explanation: Although OCR garbling is evident, the sense is of tṛpti as atyanta-pūrṇatā—perfect fullness—arising amid diverse conditions (anekatama-yukta). The teaching suggests that true fulfillment is not produced by objects but recognized as an already-present abundance of consciousness. This matches the nondual affective dimension in which experience is suffused by completeness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fire Offering in Empty Consciousness
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
महाशून्यालये िह्नौ भूताक्षविषयावदकम् ।
हूयते मनसा साधं स होमश्चेतनास्रुचा ॥ १४९ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
mahāśūnyālaye vahniu bhūtākṣi-viṣayādikam |
hūyate manasā sārdhaṃ sa homo cetanāsrucā || 149 ||
translation: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra. In the great abode of emptiness, the elements, senses, objects, and so on are offered into the fire together with the mind; that oblation is made with the ladle of consciousness.
intent_summary: The verse teaches inner sacrifice: all experience is mentally offered into the fire of empty awareness until only consciousness remains.
beginner_explanation: Imagine taking everything you notice—your body, senses, thoughts, and outer things—and offering them into a fire inside awareness. This is not a physical fire but a way to let experience dissolve into a deeper stillness. The “ladle” is your own conscious attention.
scholar_explanation: Mahāśūnya becomes the ritual altar, and bhūta, akṣi, viṣaya, and mind itself are inwardly consigned to the fire. The cetanā-sruca imagery identifies consciousness as both instrument and medium of oblation, making sacrificial process identical with absorption. This is a mature Tantric internalization of homa, where all dualistic contents are transmuted into śūnyālaya-laya.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sacrifice as Blissful Completion
sanskrit:
यागोऽि परमेशावन तुवष्टरनन्दलक्षणा ।
क्षपणात्सिधपापानां िाणात्सिधस्य पािधवत ॥ १५० ॥
transliteration:
yāgo'pi parameśāni tuṣṭir ānanda-lakṣaṇā |
kṣapaṇāt sarva-pāpānāṃ pālanaāt sarva-pārthivat || 150 ||
translation: The sacrifice also, O supreme Goddess, is characterized by satisfaction and bliss. By the destruction of all sins and by the preservation of all the worldly domain...
intent_summary: The verse concludes that the deepest sacrifice is a blissful inner fulfillment that purifies and sustains the practitioner.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that true sacrifice leads to joy, relief, and inner completeness. It washes away what burdens you and supports a stable, grounded life. In short, the highest ritual is a change in being, not just an outer act.
scholar_explanation: Yāga is here equated with tuṣṭi and ānanda-lakṣaṇa, emphasizing affective completion rather than external rite. The verse also indicates moral purification and worldly preservation, showing that inner realization does not negate life but sanctifies it. This closes the sequence by reinterpreting sacrificial efficacy as the natural radiance of realized consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Dissolution of Worship in Bhairava
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
रुद्रशविसमावेशस्तत् क्षेत्रं भावना परा ।
अन्यथा तस्य तत्त्वस्य का पूजा काश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १५१ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
rudraśavi-samāveśas tat kṣetraṃ bhāvanā parā |
anyathā tasya tattvasya kā pūjā kāś ca tṛpyati || 151 ||
translation: The absorption of Rudra into the corpse-like [limited condition] is that supreme field of contemplation. Otherwise, what worship could there be, and what could satisfy that reality?
intent_summary: He points to the highest contemplation as absorption into the absolute beyond ritual worship and objective offerings.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the deepest practice is not offering things to something separate. It is entering so fully into the truth that the usual ideas of worship and worshiper fall away. Think of it as moving from “doing prayer” to directly resting in what prayer points to.
scholar_explanation: Rudra-śava-samāveśa indicates immersion in the inert, limited, or corpse-like condition of individuality, transformed by awareness into parā bhāvanā. Bhairava denies external pūjā as sufficient for tattva because the reality in question is nondual and self-revealing. This fits the VBT’s recurring move from ritual exteriority to immediate recognition (pratyabhijñā-like intuition).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Self-Immersion in Free Bliss
sanskrit:
स्वतन्त्रानन्दविज्ञानसारः स्वात्मा हि सिद्धः ।
आवेशनं तत्स्वरूपे स्वात्मन् स्नानमीवरतम् ॥ १५२ ॥
transliteration:
svatantrānanda-vijñāna-sāraḥ svātmā hi siddhaḥ |
āveśanaṃ tat-svarūpe svātman snānam īvaratam || 152 ||
translation: The self is indeed सिद्ध as the essence of independent bliss-consciousness. Immersion in that own-nature is the supreme bathing of oneself.
intent_summary: He teaches that the true self is already accomplished as free consciousness-bliss, and practice is entering that nature directly.
beginner_explanation: You do not have to manufacture your true self; it is already there as a free, blissful awareness. The practice is to sink into it again and again, like washing off dust to reveal something that was never damaged. This is not about changing yourself, but recognizing what you already are.
scholar_explanation: Svatantra-ananda-vijñāna-sāra identifies the ātmā with autonomous consciousness-bliss, a core Trika formulation of Śiva as svātantrya. Āveśana into tad-svarūpa functions as internal ablution, paralleling the Tantric replacement of external ritual bathing with inward recognition. The verse implies that realization is not produced but re-entered.

speaker: Bhairava
title: One Worshiper, No Worship
sanskrit:
यैरेव पूज्यते द्रव्यैस्तप्यन्ते वा परापरः ।
यश्चैव पूजकः सिद्धः स एवैकः क्व पूजनम् ॥ १५३ ॥
transliteration:
yaiḥ eva pūjyate dravyais tapyante vā parāparaḥ |
yaś caiva pūjakaḥ siddhaḥ sa eko 'rth qu pūjanam || 153 ||
translation: With the very substances by which the higher-and-lower reality is worshiped, it is afflicted. But if the worshiper himself is accomplished, he alone is the one—where then is worship?
intent_summary: He teaches that when the worshiper is realized, dualistic worship collapses because the subject-object split is gone.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that if you become fully realized, the usual setup of one person worshiping a separate divine object no longer makes sense. The one who worships and what is worshiped are not two. It is like reaching the destination and no longer needing the map.
scholar_explanation: The text critiques pūjā based on dravya and external means when the pūjaka is siddha. In the mature nondual condition, pūjaka and pūjya are not distinct, so the ritual logic of offering is superseded by immediate identity with parāpara-tattva. This is consistent with Kashmir Śaivism’s assimilation of ritual into awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Breath Wandering and Returning
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
व्रजेत् प्राणो विशेज्जीि इच्छया कुवटलाकृवत् ।
दीघाधत्मा सा महादेवी परक्षेिम् परापरा ॥ १५४ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
vrajet prāṇo viśej jīva icchayā kuṭilākṛtiḥ |
dīrghātmā सा mahādevī para-kṣetram parāparā || 154 ||
translation: The prāṇa goes out and the living being enters by will, with a winding form. That long Self is Mahādevī, the supreme and lower field.
intent_summary: It directs attention to the subtle movement of life-force and its source, using breath awareness as a path to the देवी’s presence.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to the movement of breath and life energy in and out of the body. By noticing that motion carefully, you can sense a deeper presence behind it. It is like watching waves and realizing they all come from the same sea.
scholar_explanation: Prāṇa’s outward motion and jīva’s entry by icchā suggest the dynamic oscillation between manifest individuality and the underlying power of consciousness. The imagery of kuṭila, a winding or serpentine form, evokes the subtle vitality that can be traced back to Mahādevī as para-kṣetra, the field in which both higher and lower appear. The verse sits near breath-based dhāraṇās centered on prāṇa and its source.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mantra of Inhalation and Exhalation
sanskrit:
अस्यामनुचरन् वतष्ठन् महानन्दमयेऽर्ध्वरे ।
तया देव्या समाविष्ट् परं भैरवं आप्नुयात् ॥ १५५ ॥
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सकारेण िवहयाधवत हकारेण विशेत् पुनः ।
हंसहंसेत्यमुं मन्त्रं जीिो जपति वनत्यश् ॥ १५५ ॥
transliteration:
अस्यामनुचरन् वतष्ठन् महानन्दमयेऽर्ध्वरे ।
tया देव्या समाविष्ट् परं भैरवं आप्नुयात् ॥ १५५ ॥
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सकारेण िवहयाधवत हकारेण विशेत् पुनः ।
हंसहंसेत्यमुं मन्त्रं जीिो जपति वनत्यश् ॥ १५५ ॥
translation: Remaining in this rite filled with great bliss, following that Goddess, one enters the supreme Bhairava. With the 'sa' one goes out, and with the 'ha' one enters again; the embodied being constantly recites this mantra, 'haṃsa, haṃsa.'
intent_summary: It teaches a breath-based mantra practice where exhalation and inhalation become a continuous remembrance of the divine.
beginner_explanation: This practice asks you to notice the natural sound of breathing: one sound on the way out, another on the way in. Instead of treating breathing as automatic, you use it as a gentle mantra and let it carry your attention inward. Over time, the breath itself becomes a doorway into calm presence.
scholar_explanation: The verse links continuous dhyāna in mahānandamaya-ardhvare with the haṃsa mantra, where sa marks exhalation and ha marks inhalation. This is a classic prāṇa-mantra technique in which the subtle sound of breathing serves as an anugamana, an accompanying recognition of the Goddess and entry into Bhairava. The practice integrates mantra, breath, and nondual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Counting the Breath Mantra
sanskrit:
षट्शतावन वदिा रािौ सहस्राण्येकविम्शवत् ।
जपो देव्याः समुवद्दष्टः सुलभो दुर्लभो जडैः ॥ १५६ ॥
transliteration:
ṣaṭśatāni diva rātrau sahasrāṇy ekaviṃśatiḥ |
japo devyāḥ samuddiṣṭaḥ sulabho durlabho jaḍaiḥ || 156 ||
translation: Six hundred by day and night, twenty-one thousand in all—this repetition of the Goddess is taught. It is easy for the awake, but hard for the dull.
intent_summary: It prescribes a continuous daily repetition of the breath-mantra and stresses that success depends on alert awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse gives a count for the breath-based mantra practice, showing that it is meant to be done steadily throughout the day and night. The important point is not just the number, but staying aware while breathing. If you are present, the practice is simple; if you are distracted, even a simple practice feels hard.
scholar_explanation: The 21,600-count corresponds to the traditional measure of the continuous breath-cycle within a day, making japa coterminous with ordinary respiration. The verse contrasts the sulabha accessibility of the practice for the awakened with its durlabha quality for jaḍa, the dull or inert mind. It reinforces that mantra-breath identity depends on sustained awareness rather than mechanical repetition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Hidden Nectar Teaching
sanskrit:
इत्येतद्विवततं देवि परमामृतमुत्तमम् ।
एतच्च नैव कस्यापि प्रकाश्यं तु कदाचन ॥ १५७ ॥
transliteration:
ity etad vivṛtaṃ devi परमामृतमुत्तमम् |
etac ca naiva kasyāpi prakāśyaṃ tu kadācana || 157 ||
translation: Thus, O Goddess, this supreme and excellent nectar has been disclosed. Yet this must never be revealed to just anyone at any time.
intent_summary: He closes the teaching by emphasizing its supreme value and the need for discretion in transmission.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says this teaching is very precious and should not be shared casually. Some things are meant only for those ready to practice and understand them properly. It is like a rare medicine that must be given with care.
scholar_explanation: The verse marks a standard Tantric seal of secrecy: the paramāmṛta is to be guarded, not because of mere elitism, but because efficacy depends on adhikāra and inner readiness. VBT often balances universal nonduality with restricted pedagogical transmission, preserving the power of upāya by preventing premature disclosure. This transitions toward the text’s concluding cautions.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Not for the Cruel or Hostile
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
परवशष्ये खले क्रूरे अभिे गुरुपादयो् ।
वनविधकल्पमतीनां तु िीराणां उन्नतात्मनाम् ॥ १५८ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
para-śiṣye khale krūre abhakte guru-pādayoḥ |
nirvikalpa-matīnāṃ tu vīrāṇāṃ unnatātmanām || 158 ||
translation: Not for the unrighteous student, the wicked, the cruel, or the irreverent toward the guru's feet, but for the heroic, exalted ones whose minds are free from conceptual division.
intent_summary: It specifies the qualities required to receive the teaching: reverence, courage, and a mind beyond conceptual fragmentation.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the teaching is not suited to someone who is mean, disrespectful, or closed-hearted. It is meant for people who are brave, sincere, and able to look beyond rigid opinions. In other words, the container matters as much as the content.
scholar_explanation: The verse delineates adhikāra by excluding khala, krūra, and bhakta-bhakti to the guru-pāda, while admitting nirvikalpa-mati vīra and unnata-ātman. This is not moralism alone; it reflects the Tantric principle that nondual gnosis requires a sufficiently refined and integrated subject. The emphasis on nirvikalpa anticipates the text’s concern with direct, unmediated recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Giving the Teaching Carefully
sanskrit:
भिानां गुरुिगधस्य दातव्यं वनविधशङ्कया ।
ग्रामो राज्यं पुरं देश् पुिदारकुटुम्बकम् ॥ १५९ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktānāṃ guruvargasya dātavyaṃ nirvivaśaṅkayā |
grāmo rājyaṃ puraṃ deśaḥ putradāra-kuṭumbakam || 159 ||
translation: It should be given, without hesitation, to the devoted, to the lineage of gurus. [Do not give it for] village, kingdom, city, land, sons, wife, or family.
intent_summary: He instructs that the teaching be entrusted to worthy devotees rather than exchanged for worldly gains or social attachments.
beginner_explanation: This verse says the teaching should be passed on to sincere seekers and teachers, not treated like something to trade for money or status. It reminds us not to let worldly attachments control sacred instruction. The real value is inner awakening, not outer possessions.
scholar_explanation: The verse recommends dāna of the doctrine to bhakta and guru-varga while rejecting material or social compensation such as grāma, rājya, pura, deśa, and family. This reflects an ethic of transmission grounded in sincerity and lineage rather than commerce or prestige. It also signals that the text’s power is inseparable from responsible stewardship.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Renounce All, Keep the Steady Treasure
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
सिधमेतत्पवरत्यज्य ग्राह्यमेतन्मृगेक्षणे ।
वकमेवभरवस्थरैदेवि वस्थरं परवमदं धनम् ॥ १६० ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram |
sarvam etat parityajya grāhyam etan mṛgekṣaṇe |
kimeva bhairava-sthairair devi sthiraṃ param idaṃ dhanam || 160 ||
translation: Abandon all this and take up this, O deer-eyed one. For what indeed is there that is more lasting, O Goddess, than this stable supreme treasure of Bhairava?
intent_summary: He urges complete renunciation of lesser concerns in favor of the one enduring treasure of Bhairava-awareness.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava tells Devi to let go of everything else and hold to what is truly stable. This is like dropping many noisy toys to keep one jewel that never loses its value. The point is to trust the one thing that does not change.
scholar_explanation: The exhortation sarvam etat parityajya frames the teaching as the only durable dhanam, identified with Bhairava-sthairya, steadiness in the absolute. The vocative mṛgekṣaṇe softens the directive while underscoring that the real wealth is not external but the stable recognition of Bhairava. This verse effectively seals the practical section with a renunciatory nondual conclusion.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Offers Final Praise and Gratitude
sanskrit:
प्राणा अवप प्रदातव्या न देयं परमामृतम् ।
देवदेव माहदेि पवरतृप्तावस्म शङ्कर ॥ १६१ ॥
transliteration:
prāṇā avapa pradātavyā na deyaṃ paramāmṛtam |
devadeva māhadei paritṛptāvasma śaṅkara || 161 ||
translation: The breathes, life-forces, should be given away; but the supreme nectar is not to be given. O God of gods, great Lord, Shankara, we are fully satisfied.
intent_summary: Devi declares that ordinary life-force may be offered, but the highest nectar of realization must be safeguarded and acknowledges complete spiritual fulfillment.
beginner_explanation: Devi is saying that something ordinary can be shared or exchanged, but the deepest spiritual truth is too precious to be handed over casually. She also expresses that the teaching has fully satisfied her. In simple terms, she is thanking the teacher and recognizing the value of what has been received.
scholar_explanation: This closing verse affirms the distinction between expendable prāṇa and the incomparable paramāmṛta, the supreme nectar of realization. The language of paritṛpti signals complete fulfillment through direct transmission, a hallmark of tantric dialogue culminating in recognition rather than further instruction. The address to Śaṅkara emphasizes the gracious role of Bhairava as revealer of the concealed heart-essence.

speaker: Devi
title: Vijñāna Bhairava as Tantra Essence
sanskrit:
विज्ञानभैरव तन्त्रम्
रुद्रयामलतन्त्रस्य सारमद्यािधावरतम् ।
सिधशविप्रभेदानां हृदयं ज्ञातमद्य च ॥ १६२ ॥
transliteration:
vijñānabhairava tantram
rudrayāmalatantrasya sāram adyādhigatam |
siddhaśivaprabhेदānāṃ hṛdayaṃ jñātam adya ca || 162 ||
translation: This is the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, today realized as the essence of the Rudrayāmala Tantra; and today the heart of the distinctions among the perfected Siddhas and Śivas has been known.
intent_summary: Devi identifies the text as the essence of a larger tradition and says its inner heart and key distinctions have now been directly understood.
beginner_explanation: Here Devi names the teaching and says it captures the core of a much larger body of wisdom. She also says that what was hidden in different teachings has now become clear. It is like being shown the central thread that ties many teachings together.
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly frames Vijñānabhairava as sāra, the distilled essence, of the Rudrayāmala Tantra, situating it within a broader Śaiva-tantric matrix. The phrase siddhaśiva-prabhedānāṃ hṛdayam suggests that the essential point behind classifications of accomplished beings and Śiva-principles has been recognized today, i.e., through immediate gnosis (vijñāna). It marks doctrinal closure by asserting comprehension of the text’s heart-meaning, not merely its words.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Embraces Bhairava in Reverence
sanskrit: इत्युक्त्वानवन्दता देवि कण्ठे लिा वशिस्य तु ॥ १६३ ॥
transliteration: ity uktvānavanā devī kaṇṭhe līnā viśīsyas tu || 163 ||
translation: Having spoken thus, Devi, bowing down, embraced his neck and became silent in reverence.
intent_summary: Devi completes the dialogue by expressing surrender, intimacy, and silent recognition beyond words.
beginner_explanation: After speaking, Devi bows and embraces Bhairava, then falls silent. This shows that the teaching has gone beyond discussion into direct closeness and trust. Sometimes the deepest understanding is not more words, but quiet presence.
scholar_explanation: The final gesture of kaṇṭha-līna indicates embodied surrender and union, with silence (mauna) functioning as the culmination of revelatory discourse. In tantric terms, the cessation of speech points to the limits of verbal teaching and the primacy of direct presence, where jñāna ripens into intimate nondual recognition. The sequence of bowing, embrace, and silence seals the text in devotional and ontological completion.
